speechtext:
The hon. member from North Simcoe remembers well, and I venture-to think the longest day he lives he will remember the humiliating castigation which he received in this House at the hands of his friends when he undertook to Mr. CURRIE
interpret the rules of this House. My hon. friend had the selecting of his own j ury when he was on trial before this Parliament. I am sure the hon. member on a party question could not get a more desirable, a more friendly, a more biased jury than the hon. gentlemen sitting around him in this House and on the interpretation of the law, which it is the duty ,of the judge to give to the jury, I ^m sure_ that he could not get a more favourable judge than the right hon. gentleman who leads this House. But that judge, unbiased I hope at all times, but particularly unbiased on that occasion, was bound to tell the jury that there was nothing to go to them, that they were bound on the spot to give a verdict of guilty against the hon. gentleman. That is his position as an interpreter of the rules. With that wide spirit of fair play which should characterize a good Scotchman like my hon. friend, that is the record which he has in this House when bringing his great talents to bear on questions of this kind. I submit that when an hon. member on the opposite side comes before you Sir, and gives us a lecture upon what we ought to be, and what interpretation we should give to the rules, he comes not with a free and open mind, but from a fellow feeling to the protection of his friends. My hon. 'friend criticised the observations that were made in this House on Friday night and S&turdav morning. He said that the woTd 'false' was repeatedly uttered. I agree with him that possibly too often language is used in this House that is not calculated to advance and maintain the dignity of Parliament. We sometimes compare this Parliament with the courts of the country. I have every respect for the courts of this country, and I am igiad that for the last two hundred years, we have had judges who have been able to maintain their own dignity and standing and the dignity and standing of the courts. That is a matter of pride to the people and of great credit to the members of the Bar and to those who preside over our courts. But if that dignity and elevation of thought and manner is essential on the Bench, and at the Bar and to the officer of the court, I submit that they should be found in this House in an even higher degree. Cries of 'sit down,' and 'shame,' flung across from one side to the other, are not calculated to enhance the dignity of this House. I wish to call the attention of Mr. Speaker to the fact that in this House if any person is on his feet, who has no right to be standing, it is his duty and the privilege of the Chairman or the Speaker, to tell that hon. gentleman to sit down. That would be more dignified and becoming than for hon. gentlemen to yell 'sit down' to a brother mem-

ber. That is regarded as an insult and will be repelled every time it is done.
All thus is more or less aside from the question. As I understand it, as it has been so ably put before you by the hon. gentleman who moved this motion, the question is whether or not the Chairman of the committee was within his rights and whethflp he carried out the rules of the House in 3*is conduct in the Chair on Friday evening and Saturday morning. It it somewhat characteristic of hon. gentlemen opposite that if we try to discuss any question of a more or less national character, we are at once told: you are insulting the nation, insulting the flag, and insulting the individual. That as dust thrown in our eyes and in the eyes of the people to prevent us from discussing the real question. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, * and I think I speak for every hon. gentleman on this side of the House, that when we discuss the rights which we have in this House, which is the specific motion before us now, we must do so without any particular reference to the personality of the individual who .may be involved in the matter. It is a well-known principle of Christian doctrine that we can denounce sin without maligning the sinner. We have perfect freedom to condemn sin without having anything against the individual who may commit that sin. That, Sir, is the ground I take here. I am not criticising the conduct of the Chairman because of any personal spleen or feeling against that hon. gentleman. Nothing of Idle kind. But we are not to be drawn away from doing our duty in maintaining our rights in ibis House because forsooth some 'person might think we were making some personal reference to the Chairman. Such is not the case. The right of free speech, the right to represent the views of the people who send us here, and the right to carry on the business of the House in a perfectly open minded and free way, are much too important to be interfered with by any scruple as to bringing questions of this kind before the House. For that reason, I am sure that the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of Deputy Speaker, will not for a moment suppose that the bringing up of' this motion has to do with him any more than with any other individual who might have fallen into the error into which we allege he fell on the occasion referred to. 1 submit that the question of whether the hon. member for South Cape Breton could have made a speech or not in moving his motion on Friday, is<iot so very important. What really was important was the legislation which he proposed as part of the Bill before the House. That was the important thing. The hon. member for South Cape Breton represents one of the largest, if not the largest, industrial county
in the Dominion. He is here to forward as far as possible the interests of one of the great industries in his county, and he desired to forward it in connection with a subject that was in line with it. In connection with a Bill creating conditions under which steel ships the property of Canada shall be built either in this country or in the Old Country, he was legitimately and properly arguing that the industries of Canada should benefit by reason of the large expenditure of money, and that a clause should be added to the Bill providing that the industry of his county and the labour of those he represents should be utilized for the purpose of building those ships. I submit that that was a legitimate proposition, that it was his duty to bring it forward, and that it is unjustified and improper to suggest that he was making the motion for the purposes of obstruction. It was a perfectly proper and legitimate amendment. Only a few hours previously, the right hon. the Prime Minister himself* had moved as an amendment the addition of a new clause to the Bill, and if it was consistent and proper for the Prime Minister to do so after the Biil had been weeks and months under discussion, what was to prevent any hon. gentleman on this side of the House, or on the other from coming forward and proposing a seventh clause? I submit, Sir, that the amendment of the hon. member for South Cape Breton was just as legitimate and consistent as clause 6 which the right hon. Prime Minister moved to be added to the Bill.
I might point out that the fact that the Prime Minister introduced clause 6, takes away altogether the argument that undue opposition was offered. The drafting of the Bill was hardly completed when the sixth clause was added; scarcely had ;t left the hands of the draughtsman when -the guillotine and the gag were applied. The question before us is: had the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) the right to move this clause and was it desirable that he should do so. On the evening of the 8th May the Prime Minister gave notice that clauses 2, 3, 4, and 5, and the proposed clause 6 of the Bill would be the first business next day. On the afternoon of the following day the hon. member for South Cape Breton tried to get in his amendment and the Chairman ruled him out, because as he said, the first business would have to he the business of which notice had been given. That, I agree, was a proper ruling. Then began the speeches on the clauses, and we are told that we could have given room for the hon. member (Mr. Carroll) to come in with his motion some time during the day.
I find that on that day eighteen or twenty members spoke and that eight of them were supporters of the Government, and if you take the * Hansard ' columns and

count them you will find I think that as many words were spoken by Government supporters as by the members of the Opposition. The hon. member for South Cape Breton had no power to control the conduct of the House to enable him to get in his amendment. The records show that the Chairman told him that when the business then before the committee was disposed of he could get in with the amendment. I give the Chairman credit for having that in his mind, and I give the Prime Minister credit for good intentions at one stage of the proceedings, because although he did get up to move the motion that the Bill be reported, when Mr. Carroll came to his feet the Prime Minister no doubt thought of the promise made to Mr. Carroll by the Chairman the day before, and he apparently was willing to give way to Mr. Carroll to make his motion had he not been interfered with. But, the member for Portage la Prairie, who seems *to have particular guardianship over the application of the rules of the House for the last month or so, was not satisfied with the course taken by the Prime Minister and he took it upon himself to control the eye and the nerves and the feelings of the Chairman and he told him: you are noticing the Prime Minister and you are not noticing the member from South Cape Breton. Of course when the Prime Minister was reminded of the fact that a certain line had to be followed, whether there was fair play about it or not, he pressed his motion and the hon. member for South Cape Breton was deprived of the right he was promised would be given him. I submit that the Prime Minister, having heard the promise made to the hon. member for South Cape Breton that after clauses 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were disposed of, the hon. member could make his motion; in any deliberative body where fair play and honourable dealing should be supreme, the Prime Minister wak stopped from interfering with the Chairman in granting that privilege to Mr. Carroll. We are not dummies in this House; we have-the right to express our views here.
I heard the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) giving utterance to a ridiculous suggestion as to how the Speaker of this House should be governed. According to the hon. member, the Speaker is to be told to do certain things and is to be in effect merely a dummy. I never heard of such rules in any parliament, and I am sure they are not rules that govern the Speaker of this House and the Chairman of the committees. I submit to Your Honour that it is your duty to use your intellect and the voice which the Lord has given you, to tell the House how the business is to be conducted. I submit that the proceedings of the other night are deserving Mr. McKenzie.
of censure, when the Chairman refused to give Mr. Carroll the floor and when the Prime Minister pressed his motion without giving any explanation to the House. That is our grievance and that is why we submit that the conduct of the Chair, whether conscious or otherwise, was not a proper recognition of the rights of the members of this House, and therefore we were^bound to bring the matter up in order that we may know what our rights are and how the rules are to be interpreted in the future.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr Meighen) to-day laid down a rule which I never heard in this House before, that is, that if there is a motion before the House which is not debatable, the provisions of rule 15 cannot be invoked. The hon. member has been asked, aye challenged, to produce his authority for such a statement. While I give him credit for usually being very ready with his authority, if authority is available at all, it is clear that he had to let that challenge go by, and he failed to produce any authority for his statement. It is a well understood rule that, when any law or rule is calculated to circumscribe or lessen or curtail the rights and liberties of individuals, it must be strictly interpreted, and every loophole must be construed into giving the widest possible latitude to the individual. The language of the law is that there is no intentment in favour of any such rules and that every intentment is against them. You cannot read any arbitrary intention into rules, unless they show on the face of them that such arbitrary purpose is the true meaning of the rules. Unless there _ is somewhere in this book of rules which govern us, an express rule which takes away the force and effect of rule 15, I am sure that Your Honour will say that that rule must always be regarded as in force. Then there was nothing left for the Chairman to do but to drop everything before him and to put this motion. I am prepared to admit that it was not debatable since the new rules were passed. Very little time would have been lost in putting it, and no effort was made by the hon. member for St. John to debate it. Then why was it not put ? Is there any explanation why a plain, distinct and unequivocal rule of this House was violated ? I am not going to answer for the Chairman, but we must conclude, because it is the logical conclusion that comes from violation of laws in any case/that a man must take the consequences of his action. If a man does a wrong act, the conclusion of wrongful intent must necessarily be drawn from it, as far as that is necessary to carry out the wrong move that was made. I submit that the Chairman, for having refused, without any excuse or ex-

planation, to put that motion under, rule 15, was guilty of violation of his duty as Chairman and is subject to the censure of this House unless there is forthcoming some good and satisfactory explanation for the course which he took on that occasion.
I submit that the course of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in moving ,this motion is perfectly justified. I wish to repeat that the Chairman must not for one moment suppose that this is a personal attack upon him. It is simply a question of seeing to it, so far as an Opposition is capable of doing, that our rights and the rights of those who may come after us in this House shall be fully conserved under those rules, and that, whatever rights and privileges we are entitled to, shall be our property and it shall be our privilege to exercise them.
Mr. W. S. M1DDLEBRO (North Grey): Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House is a motion to censure the Deputy Speaker, first for refusing to permit the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) to add an additional section to the Bill. I desire to discuss the matter first as though the new rules had not been passed. In that case, let us see for what Teason the action of the Chairman could be censured. In the first place I submit that, when the Bill was coming out of Committee with the clause that had been added to it by the Premier, it would be quite natural for the Deputy Speaker, irrespective of anything that had been said to the hon. member for South Cape Breton in the afternoon, and irrespective of the new rules, to look to the leader of the Government to see what should be his next proceeding. I think I can say that honestly and fairly; and I believe every one will agree with me that, in a case of that kind, the getting of an important. Bill out of Committee, the Chairman would naturally take such a course. If he did anything else, he would be doing the unexpected, something different from what the Speaker of this House did when, on a previous occasion, he recognized the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. It is not for us to say whether the Speaker was right or not on that occasion. He exercised his own personal privileges and functions when he recognized the leader of the Opposition as against the minister of the Crown. In the present case, the Deputy Speaker did exactly the same thing. From that standpoint alone, had nothing else occurred, the Deputy Speaker was perfectly justified in doing what he did, and to have done anything else would have been more or less of a slight upon the Premier of this country.
In the second place, it is said that there was some sort of a suggestion in the afternoon that the member for South Cape Breton was to have the privilege of moving an amendment. The records do not show
that. On the contrary, if the Deputy Speaker were to follow what was said by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and by the right hon. the leader of the Government, he would again be perfectly justified in doing what he did. What do we find in ' Hansard '? At page 9690 we find the following remarks made by the Premier:
I might say to my hon. friend that he could move his amendment to clause 2 before two o'clock, but I do not think he could do so afterwards, and he could do it on the third reading if he desires to do so.
That shows clearly and distinctly that the Prime Minister was of the opinion that no man could move an amendment after two o'clock* on Saturday morning. What is the opinion of the right hon. leader of the Opposition? Immediately afterwards, on the same occasion, he said:
That is the puzzle. He cannot do it after two o'clock hut he cannot do it before the clause is disposed of, and if it is not disposed of before two o'clock, he is shut off altogether.
So, we have the admission of the leaders of both sides that the hon. member for Cape Breton South could not move any amendment after two o'clock, and yet this House is asked to censure the Deputy Speaker for not doing that which both leaders said could not be done.
Now, I say that even had the hon. member for Cape Breton South caught the eye of the,Speaker first, got the floor first, and moved his amendment first, yet under the new rules his motion was not debatable or amendable. It is not one of those motions which come within the definition of those which can be debated and so is one of those unnamed motions which can neither be debated nor amended. So, my hon. friend would have been in no better position had he got the floor first and moved his motion. But the question of getting the floor first is of no importance whatever. I make that statement upon the authority of the leader of the Opposition. At page 9810 of ' Hansard ' that right hon. gentleman said:
It is a matter of little importance who rose first.
The 'whole question is, the leader of the Opposition says, had the hon. gentleman a right to move the amendment? So, we can banish the question of who rose first and whether the Chairman was discourteous and so on, for the leader of the Opposition says it is a matter of little importance, and I think so too.
So, we come to the question whether the hon. member for Cape Breton South had the right to make his motion. But we do not need to go that far. We only need to go far enough to find whether we should censure the Deputy Speaker for doing what he did. He could not do otherwise under

the circumstances. He is bound to follow the rules of the House as made, and under the amended rules he would have no right to put the motion my hon. friend from Cape Breton South proposed. Now as to this second part of the motion, whether we should censure the Deputy Speaker for
* -declining to put the motion that the Chairman do now leave the Chair, as moved by Mr. Pugsley, the member for the city of St. John-
The hon. member for the city of St. John should know that, even without invoking the assistance of the new rule, the motion was not in order. In the first place, what did the hon. gentleman attempt to do? The Chairman, sitting in the chair, had put the motion, or called for the yeas and nays. But let me read from ' Hansard ':

When members have been called in, preparatory for division, no further debate is to be permitted.

speechtext: Yet the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), not more than a day of two before that, virtually said that the reason why hon. gentlemen opposite had obstructed this Bill for the last two months was that they had been offended in some way because the Government one evening proposed to put through clause 2.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.

speechtext:
That was my recollection, and I have since looked up ' Hansard ' and corroborated my view. On the 8th of May, the hon. member for Edmonton said:
I would just like to call to the remembrance of the right hon. the Prime (Minister and of the House that arrangements were made between both sides of the House for the vote up to the time when the right hon. the Prime Minister informed the House that it would have to sit until it passed section 2. It was not until my right hon. friend and his followers undertook to manage the business of this House by physical force, by establishing an endurance test in which they .failed, that there was any unwillingness shown on the part of this side of the House to come to an arrangement as to taking the vote.
And the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said practically the same thing. This, therefore, is a tacit admission that ever since that evening, about two and a half months ago, hon. gentlemen opposite have been fighting this Bill not upon any constitutional principle, not upon any principle of public policy, not in the interests of the people of Canada, 'but upon principles of political expediency only. They have said that they agreed to a vote; if that is the case they must have considered that they had before them all the necessary information and that the matter had been discussed at sufficient length to enable them to vote intelligently. It is evident, therefore, that hon. gentlemen opposite have been fighting this Bill only on the ground of political expediency, following the advice of the rough-housers who have control of the other side of the House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept any statement that my hon.	friend desires to
make in regard to the actions and motives of members on this side, but when he assumes to say to the House that we have admitted such and such a thing,
I must certainly protest. My hon. frieni did us the honour of reading ' Hansard,' and I think the House will bear me out that ' Hansard ' does not support his contention.
In regard to the resolution of censure that is now before the House, I do not think it is necessary to dwell upon it at any great length. Two statements of fact are contained in the resolution, and, so far as this discussion has gone, it is within the judgment of the House that those facts have been established. There is no doubt as the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) so * well said, that, when our friends on the other side find that the letter of the rules does not suit their purpose, they are prepared to conduct the business of the House according to what they are pleased to call the spirit of the rules. This spirit, as we know, is the spirit of control without regard to right; the assertion of the right of might. Stripped of unnecessary words, that is the position of the Government in this case. For my part, while I entirely support the resolution of censure as applied to the Chairman of -the committee, I do not want to be understood for an instant as applying the motion of censure to the Chairman of the committee and excluding from that censure the Government or their supporters in this House. The action of the Chairman was taken in accordance with the fixed policy of the Government in conducting the business of this House. On that point I want to say that the Opposition has been accused of being the cause of undue delay in conducting the business of the House, and of undue and unwarranted disorder in the House and in the committee. These are serious accusations, and I want to take this opportunity of absolutely denying them and of putting forward as evidence in support of that denial, the charge which is now before the House. We are supposed to be a deliberative body, representing the varied mind of the people of Canada, met here for the purpose of considering matters that are of the greatest importance and interest to the people, subject to certain rules of conduct and debate framed for the purpose of enabling the opinions of the people by their representatives in Parliament to be freely and fully stated. Let me diverge to say that any interference with that right of discussion and debate as applied to Parliament is an attack upon the rights and the liberties of the people who are represented in Parliament. It is with this idea in view that the rules of

Parliament were framed-the rules under which parliamentary business has been conducted in this country for many years. They have been changed from time to time, always with a view to regulating and thereby facilitating the due and proper expression of public opinion on the floor of Parliament. To-day [DOT] we have had a change in the rules and a change in the purpose of the rules; the purpose to-day being not to provide for reasonable debate and discussion in Parliament, but to place in the hands of the Government of the day the power to prevent such discussion. The hon. gentleman from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), in the numerous statements he has made to the House in regard to these rules-and we are bound to assume that he has made these statements with authority-has freely expressed that principle. He said in effect that if you did not take the power to restrict debate you could not transact the business of the House. Therefore I take it that we have on the rule book to-day a new principle, which principle expresses the right of might and the determination of the Government of the day to override the liberty of the people of Canada by preventing free discussion of matters which concern the welfare of the people of Canada in this Parliament. It is a matter well within the knowledge of the House that the assertion of this principle, this assertion of the right of might, was not because of the obstruction of public business in the way of undue discussion by members on this side of the House. There was never a session of Parliament in which there was less undue delay of public business by undue discussion than in the first session of this Parliament, and as to this session of Parliament, I say there never was a session of this Parliament of Canada in which there was less delay of public business in regard to every matter that has come before us except the one matter of the Naval Aid Bill. The Government never had an excuse, never had the shadow of an excuse.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is wandering away from the question before the House. It is not a question of what the conduct of Parliament has been heretofore, but of a particular course of action which is before the House now, and whether that action was right or wrong.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
What I wanted to,come to was that the action of the Chairman in, as we assert, violating the rules of the House was a part of the fixed policy of the Government of the day, and that the Government and their supporters are entitled to share in the censure that we believe is properly directed toward the action of the Deputy Speaker; and, in order to prove that, I have been desirous of making my
Mr. OLIVER.
case as plain as possible so that there would be no question about it. However, I take the liberty of asserting that I desire to be absolutely bound by the rules. I am speaking to-day, demanding the protection of the rules of the House, which are framed as well for the protection of the individual and of the minority as for the assertion of the authority of the majority. While I do not wish to discuss the terms or the merits of the new rules, I am desirous of showing the lack of legitimate purpose, according to the statements made on their behalf, that lay behind the introduction of these rules and that they were in fact, an assertion of the right of might and not the result of a desire on the part of the Government to facilitate the proper discussion of public affairs in Parliament. As a matter of fact, the closure rule has been introduced to protect the Government from being compelled to appeal to the country on the question of naval aid, that and that alone.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: It seems to me it is not a question why the rules were introduced; the question is, as they are now the rules of the House, whether they have been violated. It does not seem to me necessary to go behind the question to discuss the purpose of having new rules; the question before the House is whether these rules have been properly carried out.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
May I be permitted to
show that the authorities acting under the Government, before these rules were framed, violated the rules then existing, and that their violation of the practice of Parliament and of the rules of Parliament was the direct and immediate cause of such delay as did occur in tire consideration of the Naval Aid Act and such disorders that occurred in the House? It was the violation of the rules, not the maintenance of the rules, that was the cause of such delay as occurred and of such disorder as occurred. I instance that as a case parallel to that which occurred on Friday night. That is to say I do not want it to be understood that this is a mere matter of whether the Deputy Speaker saw one man or saw another man. If that is all there is in this matter we are losing the time of this House by discussing it at this length. There is more in it than that. There is the question of the protection of the rights of the individual members of this House under the rules of the House, the rights of the minority of the House under the rules of the House. What I wanted to say was that this was not an isolated case, that it was only one of a series of cases, that it was a climax, if I may be permitted to say so, arrived at in pursuance of a distinct and plain policy of the Government of the day as expressed in their rules, in the interpretation of

those rules and in the application of those rules and that they were prepared at anytime to interpret the rules literally when it suited them and in spirit when it suited them, to appeal to the letter to-day and appeal to the spirit to-morrow.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If the hon. member
implies by that, that when interpreting the spirit of the rules they were right, and when interpreting the letter they were wrong, he is clearly imputing improper motives, whichiis not allowable, and could not, of course, be permitted to pass, If he implies that the spirit and letter of the rules are the same, then I could understand him.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I think perhaps you
hardly apprehend my point. I do not see how I can arrive at a reason for what we are attempting to do unless I can give lucid and understandable reasons for it. We are asking the House to censure the Deputy Speaker. It must be established that he has committed an error or we are not entitled to censure him; we must declare that he has committed an error of judgment or an error of intent. There is no other recourse, and I am here to say that, judging from the arguments that have been made from time to time by members on the Government side and by the members of the Government in supporting actions that have been taken-I am not criticizing the Deputy Speaker in this particular, but the policy of the Government-that policy has been distinctly to follow the rules when it suited them and to break the rules when it suited them, and it is from the breaking of the rules that there has been delay in discussion and disorder in the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I must ask the hon.
member to withdraw that, because there can be nothing plainer than this fact that, if they interpret the rules to suit themselves, although they are absolutely wrong in their interpretation, that would be an improper motive. I have here Speaker Peels' decision, which says:
To impute an improper motive is not in order, and should not be allowed.
That is only one of several rulings on exactly the same line. Therefore, it seems to me that if, interpreting the letter of the rules answers their purpose at one time, and at that time they are right, and if at another time they interpret the rules by their spirit and at that time they are wrong, their motive must be an improper one, and of course that cannot be imputed to an hon. gentleman in his conduct in this House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I wish to keep myself entirely in order. I think you will concede,
Mr. Speaker, that I have tried to do so all the time. Might I be permitted to state a succession of facts without imputing motives, and let any conclusion be drawn that may be desired. I revert to the incidents of the introduction of the Naval Aid Bill. The resolution was brought forward, when the second reading came up, and it finally came to a vote. The vote on the resolution was reached by agreement, the vote on the second reading was reached by agreement, and then we went in Committee of the Whole and began to discuss the second section of the Bill. Within three hours after we had begun to discuss the second section of the Bill, we were given to understand that that section must be passed and the House would not be allowed to adjourn until it was passed. We believed that reasonable information, that reasonable opportunity for discussion on that section -upon its merits had not been given, and we felt that we would be doing less than our duty by those we represent if we permitted that section to pass on those terms and after that threat, if I am not out of order in using that word. The, discussion on that second section went on for two weeks, night and day.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: An extraordinary proceeding.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
A most extraordinary
proceeding, a most remarkable proceeding which was not at the option of the Opposition, let it be remembered, but which was at the order of the Government, an order suggested, I presume amongst the members of the Government party, and insisted upon by that party. We were given reasonable liberty of discussion on that clause during the two weeks.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: By keeping it up night and day.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I shall not enlarge upon the unparliamentary and undignified character of such proceedings; I merely emphasize the fact that it was at the order of the Government, and on the express word of the Prime Minister that the House of Commons was kept in that position for that length of time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I would like to read the resolution which is before the House, and ask the hon. member to confine himself to that resolution:
Resolved, that the action of Mr. Blondin, the Deputy Speaker, as Chairman of the Committee of the Whole House, while the committee was considering Bill No. 21, entitled, ' an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire in refusing to permit Mr. Carroll, the member for South Cape Breton, to move to add an additional section to said Bill, and also in declining to put the motion that

the Chairman do now leave the Chair, as moved by Mr. Pugsley, the member for the city of St. John, was a violation of the rules and constituted an infringement of the privileges of this House.
That is the question before the House, and the one to -which the Speaker should direct his attention.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I was in the belief, Mr. Speaker, that I was trying to direct the attention of the House to that very question. As I said in the beginning of my remarks, this is not a mere question of whether the Deputy Speaker saw one man or the other first. It is a question which affects the rights of Parliament and the liberties of the people of Canada, In order that we may understand how we should conduct debate under those rules, I think it is desirable that we should get at the very foundation of the action of the Chairman. It was in that regard that I desired to place a certain succession of facts before the House, which facts led up to the action of the Deputy Speaker. I desired to give the different steps upon vrtiich that action was finally taken on Friday night. I would appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, to permit me to follow out that line of argument. Even if I am not within the rule, there has been a considerable amount of latitude given in the debate so far, and this question is of such a character and of such importance that if we are to have a fair understanding as to the proper conduct of matters in the House it is desirable that it should be thoroughly discussed at this time and in this place. If I may be permitted, I want to be understood-

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Go on.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Order. I think that those hon. gentlemen who. dissent from the ruling of the Chair and advise an hon. member to go on are not acting within the proper lines of conduct in this House. I have only to say that it ought to be the endeavour of the Speaker to have relevancy in discussion observed, and it seems to me that it is scarcely necessary for an hon. member speaking on this motion to go back over the history of occurrences that took place week? or months before this occurrence upon which the question is based. It may be necessary sometimes to go back for illustrations, but I do not see how it can materially affect the discussion of the abstract principle.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If you rule, Mr. Speaker, that I must not proceed along those lines I shall certainly bow to your ruling and come to the point at which I desire to arrive, which is that a certain state of facts existed here on Friday night, which resulted in somewhat grave disorder in this House. For that disorder, members on Mr. SPEAKER
this side of the House have Deen specifically blamed, both by hon. members on the other side, and by the press of the country, and what I have been trying to establish, and what I would like very much to have the privilege of establishing, is that such disorder as occurred was brought about not by an enforcement of the rules of the House, but, as we understand the matter by the breaking of the rules of the House. We claim the protection of those rules in carrying on the debates of this House, and in doing so we claim that we are maintaining the right of the people of Canada to have their business in this Parliament transacted in the light of day, fully, freely, clearly and completely. To the extent to which that right is restricted, the rights of the people of Canada are restricted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
In reference to these
observations I would like to say that there is no rule better defined as to maintaining the amenities of debate, and it does seem to me that it is not becoming to endeavour to incite a member to do what the ruling of the Chair says is not proper.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure
that my friends, and you too, Sir, will do me the honour of thinking that I really do not need to be incited. I say that such disorder as occurred on Friday night was because that in the opinion of a large minority of the members of this House their rights and privileges had been unduly interfered with, and they were protesting, not on their own behalf but on behalf of those whom they represent here-and they represent within a very small fraction as many people of the Dominion as do the Conservative majority in this House.
May I allude to the fact that the new rules, the closure rules, the rules which have been made for the purpose of preventing discussion, for the purpose of protecting the Government against being compelled to face the people of Canada in an election- may I say that the excuse for these rules has been that closure rules exist in the Parliament of Great Britain. May I point out, Sir, that there is no parallel between the two cases. I will not allude to the difference in the situation of the Speaker of the English House of Commons and the Speaker of the Canadian House of Commons; it is admitted by the leader of the Government and by his friends that owing to that difference it is impossible that we could introduce the same rules here as prevail there. The closure rules were introduced in the English Parliament to overcome deliberate and intentional obstruction of the business of Parliament on the part of an infinitesimal minority of the members. The closure rules have been introduced in this Parlia-

merit, not because of obstruction but in order to protect the Government from being compelled to face the people on a question of such importance and under such circumstances that governmental self-respect would properly have called for an appeal to the people. There is no parallel between the conditions existing in the British House, which were the cause of the introduction of the closure there and the conditions existing in this House. In the British House, although they have closure, it is within the common knowledge of everyone that the Government of the day, with the closure in their hands, have appealed to the people twice within a short period in order to get from the people a mandate on questions that were not more important than the question which is now before this House for our consideration.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: They had three elections inside of three years.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
The attempt to enforce
closure in this House at this time, as it is being enforced-speaking of the rules as they stand-is an attempt of the representatives of a fractional majority of the people of Canada to prevent due discussion by the representatives of almost an equal number of the people. I take it that no such condition was ever imposed upon any parliament under similar circumstances. It is not of that we complain today; it is because the Government having seen fit to establish the right of might: to assert the right of the majority to control irrespective of precedent or equity, having established those rules, they themselves have violated those rules. I was trying to show to you, Mr. Speaker, that those rules had been systematically violated and that their violation had been the cause of the delays in the progress of this session and of such disorder as has occurred during this session. Now, Mr. Speaker, you appealed on Friday night to the members of this House for support in the maintenance of order. Everybody will agree that it is to the interest of every member and to the interest of those whom he represents that there should be order in this Chamber. But what is to be done; what is the remedy if rules are broken by those who are charged with the administration of those rules. I ask you, Sir, how is the decorum of our procedure to be maintained in the House of Commons under these circumstances? It is true that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has a solution of this question, and his solution is that whenever a member asserts his belief that he has not been fairly treated, he should be sent to accompany our present state prisoner in the Ottawa jail? I submit, Sir, that such
a suggestion will not commend itself to the wisdom of the House or to your judgment, Mr. Speaker, and is not workable in this modern era. Let me say here and now, Mr. Speaker, with all due deference both to yourself and the governmental majority that, if there is to be decorum of procedure in this House, there must be observance of the rules. These rules must be understood to be on the book for the protection of the rights of the individual and the rights of the minority as well as for the assertion of the rights of the majority. I go no further; but, if this cannot be secured in this Parliament, then there must be recourse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I entirely
agree with the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), that he is actuated by a sincere desire to observe the rules. On the present occasion he has gone into many matters which did not appear to me to be very relevant, and which did not commend themselves to His Honour the Speaker as very relevant. I am sure my hon. friend will pardon me if I do not follow him into a discussion of those matters which apparently do not touch very closely the question which is now presented for the consideration of the House.
The points which have been raised in this debate have concerned themselves with two questions, one of which might be called the practical question as to how far the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) has been prevented from expressing his views, whether by speech or by motion, with regard to the measure which has occupied the attention of the House so long. The other question, which is set forth in the motion presented by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), deals with the more or less technical question, though not less important because technical, as to whether or not there has been any breach of the rules, under the circumstances alluded to. I think all hon. members will realize one thing at least, namely, that the hon. member who occupies the position of Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees has had an unusually trying experience during the present session,^ when, on many*occasions party feeling in this House on both sides has been very greatly aroused. Speaking for myself, after a very thorough and, I hope not biased consideration of his attitude on the occasions when I have had an opportunity of observing it, I believe that he has conducted himself in a dignified and impartial manner, sometimes under conditions which would try any hon. member placed in the same situation.
Let me deal for a moment with the practical question as to the opportunity of the hon. member for South Cape Breton to ex-

press himself by voice or by vote upon this measure. There is no question that the 'hon. member for South Cape Breton had every possible opportunity of doing so. In the first place, this Bill was in committee for eighteen or twenty days. Since the new rules came into force I have always endeavoured, so far as in me lay, to have them carried out in a reasonable and fair spirit towards hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I have done so to such an extent that I exposed myself to a distinct rebuke from my hon. friend the member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark), which, in so far as it reasonably attributed to me any suggestion that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House had not had abundant opportunity of discussing this measure, I must admit was fairly well merited. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton could have moved his amendment by arrangement with his friends on the other side of the House at any time during those eighteen or twenty days. When he brought the subject to the attention of the committee a few days ago, I pointed out to him, to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, and to all hon. gentlemen opposite, that, if it were the desire, as apparently _ it was the desire of hon. gentlemen opposite, to compel us to have recourse to the amendments to the rules for the purpose of getting this Bill through committee in any reasonable time, they could still subserve that purpose and at the same time give to the hon. member for South Cape Breton the opportunity which he desired, by merely permitting one of the sub-amendments to be voted upon, whereupon he could immediately have moved another sub-amendment and there could have been no further question about the matter. Am I or am I not speaking the sober truth when I describe the situation to hon. members opposite in that way?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Is it not true that an
additional clause could not be moved until all the others were dealt with?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not quite appreciate the point I am making. There was an amendment and a sub-amendment to clause 2. I *m suggesting that, if hon. gentlemen opposite desired to compel us to have recourse to the new rules, it would have been possible for them to subserve that purpose and at the same time to give the hon. member for South Cape Breton the opportunity which he desired, by merely permitting the sub-amendment of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) to be voted upon, whereupon immediately the hon. member for South Cape Breton could have moved his motion as a subamendment to the amendment to clause 2. That was the exact situation, and I pointed Mr. BORDEN.
it out in the course of the debate. Apart from all that, it would have been competent to have brought on any of the other sections which were under consideration, in respect of two of which at least there were no sub-amendments. My hon. friend would have been in order, as I understand the rules, to have moved his amendment as a sub-amendment to any of those sections. When the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) moved his amendment on the night before we adopted the rule of twenty-minute speeches, it would have been within the power of the hon. gentleman, and in perfect consonance with the rules, to have moved his amendment as clause 7 of the Bill. In addition to that, when the motion for the consideration of the Bill as amended came up yesterday, he could have obtained every possible advantage that he could have obtained by making the motion in committee, by merely moving that the Bill be referred back to Committee of the Whole with instructions to add his amendment as clause 7. He still has the opportunity, which as he informs us he intends to exercise, of taking that course on the third reading of the Bill. Under all these circumstances, is it not abundantly apparent, not only that the hon. gentleman has had the opportunity on half a dozen occasions of making the motion to amend the Bill in the sense which he desires, but that he still has that opportunity? And that opportunity is at least as effective to him as it would have been to make his motion in committee-more effective because, in presenting his amendment in that way when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair, he has the opportunity of having recorded the vote of every hon. member, either for or against that motion. Therefore, so far as the argument of hardship is concerned, I cannot say I can appreciate it.
As to the merely technical, but important, question as to the rules, I entirely agree with my hon. friend from Edmonton, who says we must adhere to the rules, and it is our desire and intention to do so. But I do not understand that, after a motion has been made that a Bill be reported, it is possible either to move that the Chairman do leave the Chair or to move any amendment to the motion. That is my appreciation of what the rule means. My hon. friend from St. John challenged that statement, I know. But let me call to his attention what is stated by May, at page 281 of the last edition, the edition of 1906, with respect to the .corresponding motion to adjourn the House when the Speaker is in the Chair. If the House is adjourned when a debate is in progress and the debate is not adjourned, the order becomes a dropped order. Similarly, when the House is in Committee of the Whole and a motion is carried that the Chairman leave the Chair,

the order becomes a dropped order. The motions to a certain extent correspond with each other. May, in the passage to which I have referred, says:
It need scarcely be explained that such a motion cannot be made while a member is speaking, but can only be otiered by a member who, on being called by the Speaker in the course of the debate, is in possession of the House.
So you might apply that principle, which seems a very reasonable and very easily understood principle, to the proceedings of the Committee of the Whole House. Then the motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair can only be made by some member who has been called by the Chairman in the course of the debate and who when so called has possession of the committee. That seems to me a reasonable view of the practice which should be pursued in the one case and in the other.
Now, some criticism has been made upon the action which I took in rising to move that the Chairman do report the Bill. My hon. friend from Beauee (Mr. Beland) wa3 under the impression that such a motion was out of order. I will not weary the House with quotations, but if my hon. friend will look at May, page 391, he will see that that is a motion which was always required by the English rules up to 1888, and the amendment which was then made in the English rules has not yet been made in this House:
Kesohitions agreed to by a committee are upon direction from the committee reported by the Chairman to the House; and, until such report has been made, no reference may be made to it, nor to the 'proceedings of the committee. Formerly, before the Chairman could leave the Chair for that purpose, a formal question was put that he do now leave the Chair; but now, pursuant to the direction given by standing order No. 52, when he has been ordered to make a report to the House, the Chairman leaves the Chair without question put.
We still have the old procedure under which the question must be put, and, if it is to be put, it naturally follows that some person must either formally or informally-and it is often done informally-move that the Chairman do report the Bill; and I rose for the purpose of making that motion. I take full and absolute responsibility for the course I pursued on that occasion, and am ready to meet any attack or proposition of censure which may be brought forward in this House for the course I took.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
As to that motion to
report the Bill, could it be moved after two o'clock?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
It certainly could be moved after two o'clock. The clauses had all been disposed of and the Bill disposed
of, and the only course was to move that the Bill be reported as amended.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I think all you could do is to pass the clauses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I do not agree at all. The Bill had been disposed of, and the proper course to take was to move that the Bill be reported as amended, and I made that motion. I made it with a full sense of the step I was taking, and of any responsibility devolving upon me in regard to it, in view of all the circumstances connected with this Bill, with a reiteration of which I shall not weary the House at this juncture.
Some reference has been made to some supposed discourtesy towards the hon. member for Cape Breton South, as to some pledge that was given to that hon. gentleman. In the early part of that day I had pointed out to the hon. member, that, so far as I was concerned, I did not concede any right on his part to make that motion after two o'clock, and I also pointed out how it would be possible without giving away any of their rights, or their desire to have the new rules enforced, to make this motion. Some hon. gentleman said that hon. gentlemen on that side might not be able to come to an arrangement or agreement among themselves with regard to that. For that I was jn no way responsible. The debate had taken place absolutely irrespective of the section which was under consideration. It had ranged over every possible phase of the Bill, and therefore it could in no way have prejudiced the position of hon. gentlemen if one of the sub-amendments had been disposed of and the hon. member for Cape Breton South had been permitted to make the motion he desired to make.
So far as	the motion to report
the	Bill	as	amended is concerned
I think it is absolutely beyond question that that motion is not debatable. When these rules were before the House in the first instance, my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) asked me to give an illustration of motions that would not be debatable and at page 7579 of unrevised ' Hansard,' in response to his inquiry, I said:
Motions to adjourn a debate, motions to adjourn the House, or *that the Chairman do leave the Chair, or that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again; such motions which ought to be regarded as purely formal, are not under these rules to be debatable, and they are not debatable, sO far as I know, under the rules of any legislative assembly.
So, the matter was made perfectly plain in the first instance. The motion to report the Bill is of the same character. That motion not being debatable, it seems to me abundantly evident on the authority I quoted and for the reasons already given,



that the motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South was not a motion which could be entertained by the Chairman. Further than that, the motion of my hon. friend from St. John that the Chairman should leave the Chair was not a motion which could be made at that juncture.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I am glad my right hon. friend agrees with me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I only expressed surprise. I dissent altogether.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I took my right hon.
friend's observation in the usual course as assenting to the proposition-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Very far from it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: -which I have been presenting to the House. If it is not a correct proposition, of course my right hon. friend will show in what respect it is incorrect. He must go to the length of showing that if any non-debatable motion is presented when the Speaker is in the Chair then it is competent to move at once to adjourn the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Undoubtedly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
How does the right hon. gentleman reconcile that with the statement in May? Let us examine that for a moment. He says that when a non-debatable motion is before the House with the Speaker in the Chair it is competent for any hon. member to move to adjourn the House.
That is what my hon. friend said; this is what May says:
It need scarcely be explained that such a motion

That is, a motion to adjourn the House-
-cannot be made while a member is speaking, but can only be offered by a member who, on being called by the Speaker in the course of the debate, is in possession of the House.
Upon a non-debatable motion, there is no debate, and therefore the hon. member could not have been- called upon in the course of the debate.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
What does my right hon. friend make of rule 15?
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is always in order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I make of rule 15 exactly what it says, namely, that it is always in order when the member who proposes to make the motion is in possession of the House, but I say that the member must be in possession of the House before he can make it. Inasmuch as the Mr. BORDEN.
motion is not debatable, and it is not possible for any hon. member to have possession of the House, it is not possible for an hon. member to be called upon in the course of a debate which, according to the premises, is absolutely non-existent. Therefore I venture to submit that, even upon the most technical consideration of the course taken by the Deputy Speaker on the occasion referred to, he was absolutely right. Without reflecting in any way upon the sincerity of the hon. member for St. John or the hon. member for South Cape Breton, I say that the course which they took was marked by irregularity, and that the course taken by my hon. friend the Deputy Speaker of the House was marked by absolute regularity, and was, according to my conception in entire accordance with the true interpretation of the rules of this House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If the position taken by
the right hon. the Prime Minister is correct, would it not have .been much more regular for the Chairman to have ruled the motion out of order before proceeding any further?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I presume that the course which the Deputy Speaker took on that occasion was equivalent to ruling the motion out of order. My hon. friend will bear in mind that there was a good deal of excitement at the time.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: There was an emergency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: There was a good deal of excitement at the time, and hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House were making themselves very distinctly audible. I think the course the Deputy Speaker took on that occasion was one that might very well have been taken by any hon. member of this House if he were in a similar position. At all events, the point I make is that his course was in entire and absolute accordance with the rules of this House as I understand them. It does seem to me that any question which hon. gentlemen might desire to raise for the purpose of having these rules explained or better understood or debated might have been taken in another way than by introducing a motion of this character. However, we have occupied nearly a day in its consideration, and I do trust that, if it has no other result, it will at least bring about a better understanding of the rules. I repeat that in my judgment the Deputy Speaker was absolutely right in the view he took, and that he is in no way deserving of any censure of this House. On the contrary, he deserves the commendation of this House for the very dignified and forbearing course he took under circumstances that were of a very trying nature.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says he thinks

some different course might have been taken than that of making the present motion. I may say to the House that if I had been permitted to take another course, it would, as far as I am concerned, have been more in accordance with my feelings, and, I have no doubt, in accordance with the feelings of the hon. gentleman who has offered this motion. It occurred to me-and my right hon. friend surely cannot have forgotten it-that when the motion was made that the Bill, together with the amendments, be taken into consideration, it would have been quite in order for any member of the House to do as I did, namely, to move that the Bill should not be taken into consideration by the House, but that it should be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for further consideration. I was not desirous that a vote of censure should be moved against the Deputy Speaker, but I thought it of vital importance, so far as I was concerned, that the question should be considered by the House, that [DOT] the matter should be ventilated, that the rules bearing upon the subject should be examined and the matter brought to the attention of the House and the people of the country. But His Honour the Speaker was of the opinion that no statement of what had taken place in the committee could be made if it in any way called into question the propriety or regularity of the conduct of the Deputy Speaker. His Honour the Speaker called attention- I am sure my right hon. friend will make no complaint if I refer to this-to Bourinot, page 280, which says that if a member wishes to challenge the action of the Speaker-and I take it from His Honour the Speaker that the same rule would apply to the Deputy Speaker-if a member wishes to challenge his action or conduct he must proceed in the usual way, by giving notice of a motion on the subject. In connection with that statement, Bourinot refers to volume 276 of the English ' Hansard,' page 1908, and volume 277, pages 21012. As His Honour the Speaker has referred to this authority on several occasions, I think it is desirable, in order to have a clear understanding of the matter and in justification of the motion that has been made by the hon. member for Pictou, that the instances referred to by Bourinot should be cited and placed on ' Hansard,' so that hon. gentlemen may have an opportunity of considering them. I will quote first from volume 276 of the English ' Hansard,' page 1908:
Mr. A. J. Balfour:	I have not the lea^t
intention of discussing the merits of the Bill, but, simply, the attitude taken by Her Majesty's Government, and I apprehend that that will be strictly in order.
Mr. Speaker:	I can only say, in reply to
the question of the hon. Baronet, that I must defer my answer to it until the case actually 3094
arises. It will then be my duty to say whether the hon. member for Hertford (Mir. A J. Balfour) is in order or not.
Then follows a reference to two Bills relating to legislation regarding the sale of poisons-then a reference to the Indian conference, neither of which matters bear upon the subject. Then there is a heading: 'Parliament; business of the House,' and a question put by Mr. Balfour as to whether it is the intention of the Government to propose a vote on account. This is one of the authorities which Mr. Bourinot, I admit in a most careless manner, refers to as the authority for the statement that a matter like this cannot be brought up if it in any way reflects upon the Speaker or the Chairman.
