pages without reading them. His reference is to pages 810, 811 and 812. They seem to have a little more bearing upon the question but yet no direct bearing and, after all, there is very little which would justify such a statement by Mr. Bourinot. On page 812 where Lord Randolph Churchill says:
The point of order, Sir, is one of some importance and is not so absolutely hypothetic cal as it may appear. A discussion will be raised as soon as possible with respect to the grievance of the Inland Revenue clerks and in the meantime the clerks are prevented by) the Government from approaching hon. members in order to supply them with information in regard to their case. My hon. friend asks why such a prohibition is not a distinct breach of the privileges of this House.
That would have some bearing. (Reading) :
Mr. Speaker: I have no information beford me that such a prohibition has been made.
Lord Randolph Churchill:	I beg to givel
notice that I will, on the earliest opportunity, on going into Committee of Supply or on the vote for the Board of Inland Revenue, call the attention of the House to the general order of the 3rd of January issued by the Board of Inland Revenue, and will move a' resolution inviting the House to express its condemnation of the unwarrantable interference and invasion of the privileges of this House, committed by a public body.
That has some bearing, although a very remote and very distant bearing, on the question as to the proper procedure. However, it is only right that I should call the

attention of the House that it is upon these j two authorities that I was prevented from | making the motion which I made yesterday in which I sought in a different way from the motion which is now before the House to call in question the action of the Chairman of the committee. To me it did seem passing strange that one could not call the attention, as a matter of fact, to what had taken place in committee and urge that there was an error in the proceedings. However I accepted, as I was bound to do and as I did cheerfully, the ruling of His Honour, and it was in consequence of my having been unable to criticise in any way the action of the Chairman that the motion has been made by the hon. member for Pictou which is now before the House. No other course was open to hon. gentlemen who desired in any way to call in question the action of the Chairman. But the motion, it must be borne in mind, cannot be regarded as a motion of personal censure upon the Chairman. It is not that, it is a motion which is clearly applicable whether tile Chairman did what he did unintentionally or intentionally, whether he, through ignorance, violated the rules of the House or whether he violated those rules deliberately or intentionally. The resolution is as follows, and it is very important that hon. gentlemen opposite who might be desirous of seeing that the privileges of the House are not infringed upon and therefore of voting for this resolution should know its exact terms. It is as follows:
Resolved, that the action of Mr. Blondin, the Deputy Speaker, as Chairman of the Committee of the Whole House, iwhile the committee was considering Bill No. 21, entitled, ' an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective naval forces of the empire 3, in refusing to permit Mr. Carroll, the member for South Cape Breton, to move to add an additional section to said Bill, and also in declining to put the motion that the! Chairman do now leave the Chair, as moved by Mr. Pugsley, the member for the city of St. John, was a violation of the rules and constituted an infringement of the privileges of this House.
That is all. We do not ask the House to censure the Deputy Speaker; but what we do ask the House to determine is that the refusal to allow the member for South Cape Breton to move his amendment and the refusal to allow my motion to be put was a violation of the rules of the House and an infringement of its privileges. First, I shall deal generally with the importance of the subject and I think that no one will dispute that it is of enormous importance to have it ascertained, if possible, what are the rights of the minority. I do not intend to discuss the resolution which has been passed by a majority of the members in this House, a resolution in the framing of which members on this side of the House Mr. PUGSLEY.
have had no part, a resolution in the betterment or improvement of which they had no opportunity of taking any part because, by the extraordinary motion which was moved by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine in moving the previous question, all amendment has been prevented. This resolution can only be looked upon as a resolution of the majority, it cannot be regarded as a rule of the House in the ordinary sense for the reason that since Confederation, beginning in 1868, whenever it became necessary to frame rules for the Government of this House, a committee consisting of members of both sides of the House was appointed to advise Mr. Speaker in the framing of the rules. That course has always been followed from that session down to the time when this extraordinary resolution was passed. It is true that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has been able to show that on one or two occasions some unimportant motion, in favour of which no doubt there was a unanimous opinion on both sides of the House, has been adopted without going into committee; but whenever there has been any serious attempt to amend the rules of the House, I say the course has been universally followed from Confederation down to the present .session that a committee consisting of members of both sides of the House has been appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in the revision. The same course was followed in England prior to the Act of Confederation. All that you will find, with the exception, as I have said, of some unimportant matters in regard to which there would necessarily be unanimity of opinion on both sides, committees have been appointed to consider the rules of the House and to report the result of their investigations and their conclusions. I am obliged to discuss the conduct of the Deputy Speaker in the light of the resolution as the majority in this House are the ultimate court of appeal to which any member of the House must appeal. When matters are under consideration by the committee, if the Chairman makes a decision which, in the judgment of any member, is wrong, the appeal is not to the Speaker but to the members of the House. Therefore, the majority of the House, the gentlemen who framed and carried through this kangaroo and guillotine resolution, are the court of appeal to which we must go and we must abide by their judgment for the time being, at all events until their masters and ours have the opportunity of expressing their opinion upon the Government with respect to this closure resolution and with respect to all matters of public business. And, Sir, the time will come, sooner or later, when the final court of appeal, the people of this country, will have the opportunity of parsing judgment. I for one pray

that that time may come quickly. It cannot come too quickly for the proper carrying on of business, so far as Parliament is concerned, nor can it come too quickly, so far as the best interests of the people of Canada are concerned.
With regard to the motion which the hon. member for South Cape Breton desired to make, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister says in efffect: oh, it makes no difference because that hon. member might have induced hon. gentlemen on this side of the House-and I suppose he must have meant hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as well, because eight of them spoke upon clause 2-to stop speaking, even although they were limited to twenty minutes, have the vote taken on the sub-amendment to clause 2, and then he could have moved his motion as a further sub-amendment to that clause. My right hon. friend says that he might have moved his proposed additional section when the House was considering the amendment which he himself proposed and had carried through the committee, or that he might have moved it on the third reading. But that is not the question. The question is, had the hon. member for South Cape Breton the right to move his proposed section when this Bill was under consideration in the committee? Had he the right to submit that section to the committee so that it could be considered in the ordinary course, and discussed back and forth by the members of this House? If that was his right, then by the action of the Chairman he was unjustly deprived of it. Now, what were the facts, and I will only refer to them briefly because I intend to devote my attention principally to the refusal of the Chairman to recognize the motion which I made, that he should leave the Chair. What were the facts with regard to the section which my hon. friend from South Cape Breton desired to move? To begin with he did not want to move it as an amendment to clause 2. His opinion was that it could not properly be moved as an amendment to clause 2. His opinion was that as it was not relevant to any of those clauses it would properly be submitted as an additional section. He brought the matter to the attention of the Deputy Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker told him that it would be more convenient and a more proper course to move the additional section after sections 1 to 6 had been disposed of. Upon the motion of my right hon. friend, that was the first business for the consideration of the committee. Under the resolution the Prime Minister had the right to make that motion. The motion was made, and therefore no other business could be considered by the committee until those six sections had been first disposed of. But when they were disposed of, my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll), with the knowledge of the Chairman, rose to move the section which he had previously proposed
to be added to the Bill. He had the word of the Chairman, he was addressing the Chairman, and my right hon. friend, having risen, resumed his seat, and the hon. member for South Cape Breton was allowed to proceed for a short time. Then it was that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie rose to assert the right of the Prime Minister to be heard, and it was upon his suggestion that the Chairman ceased to recognize the hon. member for South Cape Breton, and made the statement that the Prime Minister had first caught his eye. By reason of that action of the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for South Cape Breton was prevented from moving, as he tod a right to do, this additional section in the committee. But it is said that that section could not be moved after two o'clock in the morning. That, Sir, I deny. The guillotine resolution only closes the door against the consideration of sections in regard to which the motion of the Prime Minister was made, and after the guillotine had fallen, so far as those sections .were concerned, I submit that the hon. member for Cape Breton had the right to move the additional section as he proposed to do. I do not wish to elaborate the argument, but I submit that in shutting off the hon. member for South Cape Breton and refusing to allow him to move the section, the Deputy Speaker was acting contrary to the rules of this House.
Now, I come to the second ground upon which I say that the Deputy Speaker acted contrary to, and in violation of, the rules of the House, that is in regard to the motion I made that the Chairman do now leave the Chair. That motion has been compared by my right hon. friend to a motion which may be made while the Speaker is in the Chair, that the House do now adjourn. I admit it is similar to that motion, but it is broader in its character, and it must be dealt with in the light of rule 15, which gives it a much greater effect than the motion that the House adjourn. Let me call your attention to the two rules. There is first the rule in regard to the motion to adjourn. You wjll find that in rule 39.
A motion to adjourn shall always he in order, but no second motion to the same effect shall be made until after some intermediate proceeding has been had.
But when the House is in committee, what is the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair? As I have said, -it is broader in its character and it must be construed according to the language of the rule. Rule 15 is as follows:
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is always in order, and shall take precedence of any other motion.
These words are not in the rule providing for the motion to adjourn when the

Speaker is in the Chair. The words, * shall take precedence of any other motion,' do not apply to the motion to adjourn.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: If a motion is always in order, must it not always take precedence of any other question?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be right as to that, and, if he is of opinion that it must take effect, let him vote accordingly. But so far as the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is concerned, those who framed the rules desired to leave it beyond the possibility of doubt, to make it clear, so clear that he who runs may read and understand, and it provides that the motion that the Chairman do now leave the Chair is always in order and shall take precedence of any other motion. What does it mean? It means that if there is any other motion before the Chair, the moment the motion is made that the Chairman leave the Chair, it shall take precedence of the other motion. I have before me the English Commons Journals of 1877, which show that the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair came a great many times before the committee and they also show the course that was taken.
The motion was made and the question put that the Chairman do report progress and ask leave to sit again. That motion was defeated whereupon the question was again proposed that the clause stand as part of the Bill.
When that motion was put from the Chair-because the question is not proposed until the Chairman -submits it to the Committee-the motion was immediately made and the question was put: that the Chairman do now leave the Chair. That is the practice which is pursued all through these various proceedings when these alternate motions were made. But, says the Prime Minister: the effect of that motion would have been to supersede the motion which was already before the Chair. So it would, that is the object of it: that is the reason the House of Commons provided long years ago that this motion could be made. It is a motion for the protection of the minority; it is made in order that the voice of the minority on important occasions may be given expression to, and that motion has always been debatable in this House until the present session. My right hon. friend says it is not dabatable under the new rules. I do not care whether it is debatable or not, my point is that it could be moved in the committee. This new rule does not take away the right to move it. I suppose that if my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who, it is generally supposed, framed these rules for the Government, had thought of it, he would have provided that it could not be moved, as he has intimated that there
Mr. PUGSLEY.
ought to be some provision that if a member questions the ruling of the Chair he ought to be imprisoned. If the hon. gentleman thought of it, he would have provided that if any member of this House dared to question the ruling of the Chair he should be imprisoned for a term of not less than twenty years. The hon. gentleman has said that I got off with flying colours because the Chairman ignored me and that if I got my deserts some severe punishment would have been meted out to me. Fortunately it did not occur to the Government or to the hon. member to frame a resolution so drastic in its character that it would prevent a member of the House from questioning the ruling of the Chairman or of Mr. Speaker.
I submit that the Prime Minister having moved that the Bill be reported, before the division was taken upon that motion it was the.right of any member of the House to move that the Chairman leave the Chair, and had that motion carried, it would have superseded the motion made by the leader of the House. Whether it would carry or not is not the question; the question is as to my right to move the motion at the time I did, and I say that under the rules of the House there can be no question as to that. What took place at the time ? It appears from ' Hansard ' that before the 'Chairman called for the yeas and nays, and when he was about putting the question, I moved that he leave the Chair, and it was the duty of the Chairman to put my motion. I did put the motion that the Chairman now leave the Chair, some few minutes, as appears by ' Hansard,' before the Chairman asked those who were in favour of the motion to say ' yea ' and those against it to say ' nay.' It clearly appears, according to ' Hansard,' that I made the motion in proper time, and that I made it in accordance with rule 15; and it was the duty of the Chairman to recognize my motion and put it to the oommittee.
I say, further, and I say this with a full sense of my responsibility as a member of the House, that the Chairman did actually put to the committee, or proceeded to put to the oommittee, my motion. He said: 'The motion is, shall the 'Chairman leave the Chair.' Whether from his own intuition and without suggestion, I am not prepared to say, but he immediately corrected himself and put the other motion that the Bill be reported. That shows you, and ' Hansard ' also shows, that the motion was before the Chairman; it shows you that the Chairman knew of the motion. I was standing here close to him and it was utterly impossible he could not have heard my motion, and having heard that motion made in accordance with the rules of the House, and without pointing out

to me that he deemed it to be out of order, in violation of the rules of the House, he deliberately ignored the motion; he deliberately violated the rules of the House, and he proceeded to put the motion moved by the Prime Minister that the Bill should be reported.
Unless the majority in this House, who are in the position of final judges in this matter, are prepared to say that the Chairman shall be allowed with impunity to violate the rules of the House, surely they must vote for the motion my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has presented. If, upon the other hand, they have so little regard for the honour and the dignity of this House; if it be true that they have so little regard for the rights of the minority, that they are prepared to justify the Chairman in deliberately violating the rules, then I take it they will vote against this motion. Whatever be the fate of this motion, we on this side of the House will feel that we have discharged our duty according to the best of our ability. ' Hon. gentlemen opposite may think it is all right for the majority to rule and to break through the usages and precedents of this House, but let me tell them that such a course will not commend itself to the people of Canada. If they are prepared to justify the_ breaking of this rule, why will they not justify equally the breaking of other rules, and if they are prepared to do that, then I ask you, Sir, what was the use of their degrading Parliament by passing the closure resolution? What was the use of that long continuous session extending night and day over fourteen days; why did not they rely upon a Chairman who would be willing to do what they tried to do on that memorable Friday night:	break the rules
and declare the Naval Bill carried ? Why should the Chairman not refuse then, as well as upon the occasion to which we are now referring, to recognize members on this side of the House? Why should he not have just as deliberately turned his back on those who sought to move amendments and have declared the clause carried? Why should he not have proceeded then to clauses 3, 4, and 5, have declared them also carried and have deliberately refused to recognize members on this side of the House? It would have been just as excusable, just as justifiable to have done that as to have acted as he did upon the occasion to which this resolution refers. Therefore, for these reasons which I have endeavoured briefly to present to the House, it seems to me that every hon. gentleman who has a proper regard for the rules and usages of Parliament and for the preservation of the rights of the minority, must feel constrained to vote for the resolution. It does not necessarily imply that the Chairman has deliberately violated the rules of the House; but that he has violated them, whether intentionally or unintentionally, I think goes without saying.
My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) has sought to make an excuse for the Deputy Speaker upon the ground that this has been a trying session; that upon occasions when the Deputy Speaker was presiding there was excitement and confusion. That is true; but if a Chairman or the presiding officer of any assembly keeps his head and seeks to give fair play to everyone and a reasonable opportunity to the minority to express their views, if he has always before him as a shining light the rules which govern the House and adheres to them and gives to every hon. member the opportunity to avail himself of them to a reasonable extent, then there will be no difficulty.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Before proceeding to
conclude the remarks which I intend to make upon this motion, I think it proper that I should call the attention of the House to the fact that Your Honour has brought to my notice the decisions of Speakers Denison and Brand of the English House of Commons to the effect that the proper way to challenge a decision of the Speaker or the Chairman is by a motion similar to that now before the House, and that it cannot be done except by motion. I have not bad an opportunity of looking into the decisions, but the notes would indicate good authority for the course which Your Honour has stated to the House as the correct one.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) and also some other hon. gentleman, either the Prime Minister or the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) took the ground that a motion that the Chairman leave the Chair cannot be made when there is a non-debatable motion before the committee. It may be that when the Government framed the resolution they thought it would be desirable that it should so provide, but the resolution does not so provide and leaves rule 15 just as it was before. To carry out the view of these hon. gentlemen it would have been necessary to amend rule 15 so as to read:

A motion for the Chairman to leave the Chair is always in order and shall take precedence of every debatable motion.
But that is not the rule, and that rule has not been amended by the new rule that was adopted. It may be that under a strict construction of the new rule, such a motion is not debatable, but that does not prevent it being put. It is one thing to have a motion debatable and another thing to have the right to place it before the committee, and the right to present that motion has not been taken away; it exists to-day as it has existed for generations in the British House of Commons and in this House. And, just as has always been the case it takes precedence of any other motion.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Even a non-debatable
motion?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Yes; for the reason that the rule does not say ' non-debatable.' Let me read the rule to the Postmaster General and ask his careful consideration of it,- because I should be sorry to think that a majority of members of this House would sustain a violation o,f the rule. The majority, as I lave said, is the court of appeal, and the court of appeal should not decide a question as a party question, but 'Should endeavour to ascertain and determine what the rule is, an l if there lias been a violation of the rule, the majority should not hesitate to say so. The rule as it has stood for a long time is:
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is always in order, and shall take precedence of every other motion.
Now, the Prime Minister has taken the ground that it was necessary for him to move the motion that the Chairman report the Bill. That being so, this motion that the Chairman leave the Chair took precedence over that motion. It superseded that motion for the time being. *

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Does it not strike my hon. friends as reasonable that the wording of rule 15 must be construed as referring to a motion that is under debate?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Because if a motion which is not debatable is put in the hands of the Chair-Speaker or Chairman-that motion must be put forthwith. That being the case, another motion cannot be put in its place.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Why not? Where would be the difference between that case and the case of a motion which had been fully debated, nobody else wishing to speak on it, and the time having arrived when the question should be put? Before the yeas and nays are called the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is in order. That right is to be taken away.
Mr. PUGSLEY.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: How can that be if under the rules no man is to rise after two o'clock?

Except to
move to report the Bill. That is covered by the practice of Parliament.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.

There is no 'except'
about it.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.

The rule says:
And if such adjourned debate or postponed consideration shall not have been resumed or concluded before two of the clock in the morning, no member shall rise to speak after that hour, but all such questions as must he decided in order to conclude such adjourned debate or postponed consideration shall be decided forthwith.
If my hon. friend from Calgary is right, the only thing that could be done after two o'clock was to conclude the consideration of the six sections then before the committee. If that' be so, the Prime Minister could not move that the Chairman report the Bill, because he had to rise in order to do so. Does it not seem that upon these sections or resolutions, in regard to which the guillotine notice has been given, no member can speak after -two o'clock, and that, with regard to any other question which may be raised, and in respect of which the guillotine notice has not been given, that does not apply? It was quite in order for my right hon. friend to rise and make tire motion which he did after two o'clock; it was quite in order for me to rise and move that the Chairman leave the Chair, although I made the motion after two o'clock, because the two o'clock restriction applies only to those resolutions or sections in regard -to which the minister has given notice.

Did the
notice not cover the Bill in its entirety, and, as it covered the whole of the six sections, was it not obvious that the notice was sufficient to put the Bill out of committee?

No, it did not. The
notice was that the consideration of sec-

tions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 shall be the first order of business, and shall not be further postponed.

The notice does not
say the whole Bill; it does not include the title.

speakerposition: Postmaster General

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: It is entirely operative, but not operative to the extent to which my hon. friend thinks it should be. The trouble with my hon. friend and the gentlemen associated with him is that, having got a taste of blood, they seem to hunger for more. Having been able to get six sections through under closure, they think it a monstrous thing that they cannot do whatever else they think desirable. It is making fine progress to dispose completely of six sections on one day's notice; that shows the kangaroo to be jumping rather fast. In twenty-four hours he jumps through the whole Bill-the kangaroo is a mighty powerful animal.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it is not a kangaroo at all.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Yes, it is; because of
the powerful hind legs of the animal, it leaps ahead with wonderful vigour. How could anything leap ahead more quickly than this Bill during the twenty-four subsequent hours to the notice given by the Prime Minister?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: That is not a kangaroo.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: In this case it would be the fox fighting the kangaroo.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
It would be intellect
against brute force. Rule 15 says:	.
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is always in order, and shall take precedence of any other motion.
The Prime Minister rose and moved that the Chairman report me Bill, and before the yeas and nays were called upon that motion, I moved that the Chairman leave the Chair. Under rule 15, that motion should have taken precedence over any motion then before the committee. I cannot for the life of me see how it is possible to give any other interpretation to the rule. What did the Chairman do? It has not been suggested by anybody that the Chairman was not aware of my having made the motion. It is admitted that the Chairman
knew that my motion was made, but he deliberately declined to put that motion to the committee, and he did so in violation of the rules of the House.
The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) made an extraordinary statement just before he concluded his remarks. He referred to the obstruction and disorder, which he said was attributable to the rough-houses.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Rough-housers.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
That is an expression
with which I am not familiar. Let me say to my hon. friend, however, that during the long and somewhat strenuous fight that has been waged from this side of the House against the Naval Bill, the provisions of which we do not believe to be in the best interests either of Canada or of the Empire as a whole, there has been no distinction on this side between one member and another. We have fought together, side by side, in the heartiest comradeship, always animated by a- desire to meet the views of and support the distinguished leader whom we are so proud to follow. I am happy to believe that what has been done on this side of the House has been done with his hearty approval. We have taken the stand which we have, and we have fought the fight as we have on this side of the House, not in the hope of any personal gain or advancement to ourselves, but because we believed from the bottom of our hearts that we were fighting in the best interests of our country and in the best interests of the Empire of which Canada forms so important a part. Now that, after the application of what I shall call, without being unparliamentary, brute force, we have been brought so near the close of the fight,' let me express the hope that, even although we may be powerless to prevent this unjust and improper measure from becoming law, the Government may consider that it will not be desirable to bring this proposed measure into operation. Animated, as I would hope they would be animated, by a feeling of self-respect, I would think that the Government, without any undue delay, would dissolve this Parliament and obtain the opinion of the people in regard to their naval policy.
Reference has been made to the fact that when the Chairman made the report to you, Sir, last Saturday morning, I used harsh language when I said that the Chairman was making to you a false report. It may be that the language was harsh; it may be that in a calmer moment I would have selected other language in which to express the views which I entertained in regard to that report. But when you come to judge my conduct, Mr. Speaker, in making use of that language, I want you to bear in mind that for months the Government have been seeking by means which we on this side of the House consider to be most un-

fair, to have that measure passed; I want you to bear in mind that as long ago as the month of March the Government decided to carry the measure or, at all events, one clause of the measure, before any opportunity was given to the committee to rise. I want you to bear in mind that various Chairmen, I cannot believe acting independently, I cannot believe but what they were acting with the full knowledge and at the request of the Government, even went so far as to seek to violate the existing rules of the House in order to carry the measure through and, Sir, at last, after we had been compelled to stay here in our seats day after day and night after night, fighting for what we believed to be the interests of our country, fighting for the liberty of Parliament, fighting for the rights of the people whom we represent and endeavouring to prevent the rules of the House from being violated, after that, Sir, after that most strenuous attempt to carry the measure through by a violation of the rules, the Prime Minister was compelled to rise in his place and say that under the rules of the House they would not be able to make progress which they had hoped for and had deliberately set out to accomplish. Then, Sir, bearing in mind that in the middle of the fight, in the midst of all the excitement which their conduct had caused, they sought to change the rules of the House which should govern the debate and the progress^ of legislation, bear in mind, Sir, that they did not proceed in the ordinary way by appointing a joint committee to assist Your Honour to revise the rules but determined to do it by a resolution with Your Honour in the Chair. Bear in mind, too, that after the right hon. the leader of the Opposition had risen in his place and Your Honour had recognized him, the Minister of Marine, a member of this Government, was put up for the purpose of preventing my right hon. friend from exercising the right which undoubtedly belonged to him as leader of the Opposition to address the House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is rather wandering away from the question before the House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: But I was answering the hon. member for Portage la Prairie who said, and said, if I remember aright, without rebuke from Your Honour, that my course was scandalous in speaking of the Chairman of the. committee as I did.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is not exactly correct there, because I rebuked the hon. member and asked him to withdraw the expression.
Mr. PUGSLEY.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Upon the objection
of an hon. member on this side of the House and then he was allowed to use the expression ' outrageous ' which is not very different from the expression 'scandalous.' However, that being so, do you not think that I had the right to explain the reason why I used the language? It will take only a moment. At last, when he found the Chairman, the Deputy Speaker of this House, appointed by the Government to that position, deliberately violating the rules governing this House, rule-s which have heretofore prevailed and been respected, can you wonder that I used the language which I did? But my hon. friend has said that if I had used that language to a judge of this land I would have been now behind prison bars, expiating imy offence by being deprived of my liberty. Let me say to my hon. friend that for forty years I have been pleading in the courts of this country and I have pleaded before judges who were fair and impartial and I have pleaded, I regret to say, before judges showing a disposition entirely opposite of_ that and when I found judges who were not animated by a disposition to do fairly by the litigants who came before them, I have never hesitated to tell those judges what I thought of their conduct, and the men pleading at the Bar of this country who would be afraid to tell a judge what he thought of his actions, if those actions were improper and unjust, would be unworthy of the position which he occupies as a member of the Bar of this country. I have never hesitated and have never been afraid to do that. I have a great respect for these 'high and honourable positions, but in my judgment these positions are made lofty and honourable by the manner in which the duties are discharged by those who occupy them for the time being. Let me express the hope that no fear of imprisonment, no fear of any penalty which, by possibility, could ever be imposed upon me, will ever deter me from doing what I deem to be my duty to the people whom I represent and to the people of this country.
Hon. CHARLES J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice): I desire to speak only for a few moments, and during those few moments to devote myself to the question that is now before us. I would be sorry to say one word which might be of a nature to diminish the perfect and complete satisfaction with himself which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) has devoted the concluding portion of his remarks to persuading this House he entertains. It did seem a little irrelevant, and there must have been a pressing necessity bearing in upon the mind of -the hon. gentleman when he found it necessary in connection with this motion to protest to us the perfect unanimity and

unquestionable harmony -that, throughout this debate, has prevailed on the other side of the House. That fact-I take his statement to be a fact-is after all perhaps only an illustration of how absolutely deceptive appearances may be; and perhaps the hon. gentleman felt the great necessity of impressing upon us that fact which bore upon him; because, after all, he has some responsibility for some of those appearances which it turned out were so deceptive.
I want to say a few words on what, after all, as I understand, is the one question that presents itself upon this motion. I was glad to note that the hon. gentleman In opening his remarks pointed out that this motion did not necessarily involve the imputation of any blame as for intentional wrongdoing to the Deputy Speaker of this House. I would have been more glad, and it seems to me it would have been more fair upon his part, if he had come forward frankly and disavowed the .intention of Making any such imputation; because, whatever else may be said about this matter, I think that the hon. the Deputy Speaker of this House can, with perfect confidence, rely upon the fact that his conduct, as we all witnessed it on the evening which he was called upon to give the decisions which are now complained of, was that of a man acting with perfect fairness and perfect impartiality in the desire to carry out the rules as he understood them.
Now, the hon. gentlemen dwelt principally upon that allegation of his motion which complains of the action of the Deputy Speaker in refusing to entertain and to put the motion that the committee do now rise, which the hon. gentleman made on the occasion that has given rise to this discussion.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: The motion I made was that the Chairman do now leave the Chair. The difference is quite important.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I beg pardon; the hon. gentleman's motion was that the Chairman do now leave the Chair. He passed over very briefly that portion of the motion which complains of the decision of the Chairman with regard to the motion which the hon. member for South Cape Breton desired to make on that occasion. I am . not surprised that he should have done so. In connection with that motion, something has been said in the way of imputing unfairness, because of the point of order that was raised with regard to it, and because of the decision that was given upon that point of order. So far as complaint has been made, or may be made, on the ground of unfairness, as distinguished from complaints that the rule was not correctly interpreted and applied, it seems to me that that complaint is manifestly and unquestionably without foundation. We all remember that after the hon. member for South Cape Breton had put forward his motion, and after the point of order had been taken that it was not admissible in view of the fact that the right hon. leader of this House had already seized the committee with a motion, and some reference had been made to some occurrences earlier in the day, when it had been suggested that at a later period the hon. member might move the amendment he desired to make, the right hon. leader of this House, as a matter of courtesy, offered to withdraw his motion and allow the hon. member-

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: He did so on conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell me what the conditions were?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If you look it up,
you will see.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
That is not
the point. We do not want courtesy; we want our rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: That is just the point I want to make. The right hon. gentleman said that he did not want courtesy-that he did not want to have anything by courtesy.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
On what possible
grounds do hon. gentlemen complain of unfairness in being prevented from doing a thing which they were offered an opportunity to do by courtesy, if they will not take that opportunity?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: We only want to do what we have a right to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
They insist on the
application of the rule.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: So that the one question that can arise here is whether the rule was correctly interpreted and applied. There can be no possible question of unfairness in connection with it.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: There certainly was.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
We were willing to
waive the rule, and surely there could be nothing fairer than that; but hon. gentlemen said no, we must have the rule, and then when it turned out that the rule which they insisted on having applied did not allow the motion to be made, they say it is unfair. Mr. Speaker, it may be open to discussion whether the rule was correctly interpreted or not, but surely there could have been no element of unfairness in the decision upon that rule, or no element of unfairness inspired by a desire to prevent

tile making of an amendment. All fairness was offered to the hon. gentleman and his right hon. leader refused to have it as a matter of courtesy. .
Now, in regard to the question relating to that motion I do not propose to detain the House. If there is anything clear in the rule, which was adopted for the purpose of enabling debate to be closed after a reasonable time, it is that the motion which the right hon. leader of the House had made was a motion not susceptible to debate or amendment, a motion which, under the rule, must imperatively be decided without debate or amendment. That being so, it seems to me that it was the manifest and imperious duty of the Chairman to put that motion without listening to debate, or without affording an opportunity for amendment. But, as I have said, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) directed his attention principally to that portion of the motion which complains that the motion he sought to make, that the Chairman do leave the Chair, was not entertained and was not put. He based his argument in support of that complaint upon article 15 of the rules as they now stand, and he seemed to think that there was some distinction or difference under rules 15 and 39 between a motion, made in committee, that the Chairman leave the Chair, and a motion to adjourn the House made before the House. There is a difference in the words. The one provides that the motion for the Chairman to leave the Chair is always in -prder, and ^hall take precedence of any other motion, and the other rule 39, dealing with the motion to adjourn, simply declares it to be always in order, and does not add the other words. I must confess it is difficult for me to see what practical distinction results from this difference in words, because if the motion to adjourn is always in order, it must necessarily follow that it must be received, and the House must proceed to deal with it, even if there be another motion pending. So that while the words are more explicit in one case than in the other, I entirely fail to see that there is any substantial difference between the two provisions. If you look at the authorities, who have interpreted these rules, you will find it laid down absolutely that the one is the equivalent of the other. If you look at page 524 of Bourinot you will find it laid down there. Bourinot says:
Kule 77 of the House of Commons provides: < a motion that the Chairman leave the Chair shall always be in order, and shall take precedence of any other motion/ If this motion (which is equivalent in its effect to a motion for the adjournment of the House) be resolved in the affirmative, the Chairman will at once leave the Chair, and no report being made to the House, the Bill or question disappears' from the order paper.
Mr. DOHERTY.
So we have the one motion declared to be absolutely the equivalent of the other.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Will the hon. minister
read from the previous page, at the bottom, beginning, 'The Speaker will then say'?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
The Speaker will then say: ' when shall the committee have leave to sit again ' ? A time will then be appointed for the future sitting of the committee. But if a member -wishes to supersede a question entirely he will move ' that the Chairman do now leave the Chair/
And, if a member wishes to supersede the matter that is before the House when the House is sitting, he will move the adjournment of the House, and if that be carried the question is superseded. As the author says, one motion is the equivalent of the other. That being so, let us look at' what the two motions are; what they are in 'their nature and in their effect, and I think that when we have ascertained that we will see just how completely the effect tought to be attached by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to rule 15 gives way, in view of the effect of the amendment to rule 17 under which we were proceeding on the occasion in question. It will not be denied, I think, even by the bon. member (Mr. Pugsley) that rule 15 and every rule contained in the rules of this House is affected by the subsequent passing of this amendment to rule 17, to this extent: that everything in any existing rule which may be found to be inconsistent with the provisions of the amendment to rule 17 is by that amendment repealed and overridden. I do not think that proposition will be disputed for a moment. Not only is the provision amending rule 17 subsequent in time to this rule 15, but it is furthermore a rule dealing with a specific condition of affairs. Rule 15 is a general rule; a rule made in general terms for application generally. The amendment to rule 17 is not merely a subsequently enacted law which therefore repeals -anything inconsistent with it contained in previously existing law, but it is a rule made to have application to and to govern a special and particular case. It is just as elementary a maxim of the interpretation of law, from the point of view of the repealing effect of one law upon another, that a provision made for a specific case overrides a general rule, as it is that a subsequent law overrides previously existing law inconsistent with the provisions of that subsequent law. Let us look at the condition with regard to these motions as it was before the new rule. As the leader of the House pointed out this afternoon, quoting from May, while a motion to adjourn is always in

order, that does not mean that a man may rise when another man has the floor and interrupt him for the purpose of making a motion to adjourn. A motion to adjourn may be made by a person who has been recognized and called upon by the Speaker in the course of the debate. Bourinot says substantially the same thing as the Prime Minister laid down this afternoon, and Bourinot points out just when a motion to adjourn could be made and could be made irrespective of this amendment to rule 17. He says:
A motion for the adjournment of the House may be made while a matter is under discussion or in the interval of proceedings.
There are, therefore, two occasions on which such a motion can be made irrespective of the amendment to our rules; that is to say: while a matter is under discussion or in the interval of proceedings.
In the first case (when the motion is made, when a matter is under discussion) such a motion is in the nature of an amendment, and in the other it is a substantive motion to which a reply is permitted to the member who makes it.
Let us apply that to the situation as it was when the hon. member for St. John started to make his motion that the Chairman leave the Chair. Was that motion made while matter was under discussion? Manifestly not. It was made at a time when a matter was before the committee that was not susceptible of discussion; a matter that under the amendment to rule 17 was not susceptible of discussion and at a time when a motion had been made which under the terms of that rule must be decided. The words are:
-shall be decided without debate or amendment.
So that most certainly it was not made at a time when a matter was under discussion. Was it made during an interval in the proceedings? There was no interval in the proceedings. It was made at a moment when the Chairman was engaged in performing the duty that this rule 17 imperatively imposes upon him. That rule ordered him to have the motion of the Prime Minister decided without debate or amendment. He was proceeding to have that question decided; he had asked for the yeas and nays.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Oh, no. My motion was before he asked for the yeas and nays.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
He asked for the
yeas and nays the second time after he had been interrupted, but the motion was made after he had called for the yeas, and nays the first time.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Well, we will read it
again from ' Hansard ':

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I am now putting the motion that the Bill be reported.
Some hon Members: Shame.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Those in favour of the motion will please rise.
Mr. Pugsley: I move that you now leave the Chair.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Read on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Read on, says the hon. member. Does he mean to say that anything that happened afterwards could alter the fact that when he made the motion the Chairman was engaged in saying: Those who are in favour of the motion will please rise? Will that fact be altered by anything that happened afterwards?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
pardon me. Does he not know that the proper form is:	Those in favour of the
motion will say aye. I had made my motion that the Chairman leave the Chair just before that occurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: The question had been put.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Not properly put.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Oh, not properly put;
that is a new argument.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: And therefore, it had not been put at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: At that time thei e was just one proceeding that could go on, that was the putting of the question. Anything else was a violation of the rule. The rule is absolutely imperative. If the Chairman were not proceeding as best he could in the face of the interruption to put that question, he would be susceptible of censure, because there is an imperative law of Parliament not merely that the Chairman shall put the question and then wait to hear discussion, but that the question shall be decided, that is, the vote taken and the question decided without debate or amendment. Inasmuch as there could be no debate, there was no opportunity for the moving of this motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair during the course of the discussion. Therefore, as pointed out by the right hon. the leader of the House (Mr. Borden) this afternoon, there was no occasion when that motion could be made, because it could only be made during the course of a debate. This rule moreover precludes the Chairman not only from listening to anything in the nature of a debate but from listening to anything in the nature of an amendment.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Did not my hon. friend read a moment ago from Bourinot a statement that the motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair may be a distinct substantive motion and not an amendment? My motion was not an amendment; it was a distinct substantive motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: It may be a substantive motion but then it must be made in an interval of the proceedings.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: My motion was made during an interval of the proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I shall come to that
matter in a moment. I am giving my hon. friend his opportunity. He had two opportunities. The motion might be made during the course of the discussion. I think I have made it abundantly clear that there was no opening for him there, because under the rule there could be no discussion. Not only was this motion not susceptible of being made then as a motion pending a discussion, because there was actually no discussion going on, but the seeking to make this motion was in direct violation of the rule because, as pointed out by Bourinot, the motion itself is in the nature of an amendment, which the rule expressly precludes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman says; hear, hear. Mr. Bourinot will stand the irony of the right hon. gentleman. I think I can stand my own share of it because I think it can be pointed out, so that anyone can see, just how correct Mr. Bourinot is.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I rise to correct my
hon. friend. Bourinot, from whom he quoted, says that it need not necessarily be in the nature of an amendment, but that it may be in the nature of a substantive motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will possess his sou! in patience, I shall come to that in a moment. Mr. Bourinot says that there are two occasions on Which this motion may be made. It may be made during the course of a discussion and it may be made as a substantive motion. I shall come to the question of a substantive motion in a moment.
This is in respect of the question whether it is made pending a discussion or not. If there be a matter before the House and I rise to move that the Chairman do leave the Chair, is it such a very absurd proposition to say that my motion is in the nature of an amendment ? What is the effect of any amendment P It is to set aside the proposition that is before the House and to substitute something else for it. When a motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair comes in the course of discussion, what is the effect of that motion, if it be not that the House do not adopt the motion that is proposed, but in lieu of it the motion that ' the Chairman do leave the Chair, and that the measure thereby is killed. Mr. Bourinot is clearly right when he says that this
Mr. PUGSLEY.
motion is in the nature of an amendment. I do not say that it makes any particular difference, but perhaps this very instance is the clearest ilustration of how absolutely the motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair may, at all events in effect, be an amendment. What was the motion that was before the committee ? It was tnat the Chairman do report the Bill. That necessarily implied that the Chairman leave the Chair and report the Bill. The motion of the Ihon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was that the Chairman leave the Chair, dropping the words ' and report the Bill,' so that the motion on its face was to strike out the words and report the Bill.' It was most manifestly and unquestionably in this ease an illustration of the general rule that a motion to adjourn pending a discussion is in the nature of an amendment. Therefore, under rule 17 as amended, that motion was clearly not receivable, not only because there was no debate in the course of which it could be made, but because there could be no amendment to that motion, and the motion that the Chairman do leave the Chair was in the nature of an amendment.
The hon. gentleman says there may be a substantive motion made to adjourn the House.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I did not say that. I
said that my motion that the Chairman leave the Chair was a substantive motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Bourinot deals with
the motion to adjourn as a substantive motion. While it is true that he says that the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is equivalent to a motion to adjourn the House, his remarks immediately following what I read above can only refer to a motion made while a matter is before the committee for the purpose of discussion with the view of arriving at a report to be made to the House. If the hon. gentleman will read a little further, he will see how clearly that is brought out. (Reading):
Motions for the adjournment of the House or of the debate are generally made in the Canadian Houses in the course of a discussion, in order to give an opportunity to members who have already spoken to speak again, or to make certain explanations which, otherwise, they might not be able to make.
Substantive motions for the adjournment of the House ought to be reserved for occasions when it is necessary to discuss questions of gravity. They are not unfrequently proposed in the Canadian Commons with the view of bringing before it some question in which a member is immediately interested.
In other words, the motion which he has in contemplation, when he so speaks of a substantive motion, is the motion provided for in the second and following

paragraphs of rule 39; that is the motion to adjourn that is made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. That is not in any way assimilable to the position here. This motion made here was one that purported to be made while a matter was under discussion and consideration. As a matter of fact, at the time that this motion was sought tq be made, there was under consideration before the committee the motion that the Chairman do report the Bill, so that this motion can stand, if it can stand at all, not as a substantive motion to adjourn, but as a motion made in place of another motion pending before the committee with the view of substituting for that motion other action on the part of the committee, which would have the effect of defeating that motion and of killing the measure before the committee. So, for both these reasons-because there was no discussion during which this motion could be made and because this motion was necessarily of the nature of an amendment- the motion which the hon. member sought to make was in direct violation of rule 17, and the Chairman could have no alternative but to refuse to hear the motion or entertain it for a moment.
Now, some suggestion of complaint was made because the Chairman did not proceed to rule the motion out of order, and then go on, if he were right in doing so, to put the question. I submit that, inasmuch as all imputation of discourtesy is repudiated by hon. gentlemen, there is no room for dispute on that point. I do not think that courtesy requires the Chairman to do anything but observe the rule. But, even if it could be suggested that he could haye departed from that to explain to the hon. member that he would not entertain his motion under the circumstance, surely complaint cannot be made on the ground of discourtesy because such an imputation is repudiated by those who have presented this motion.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Does the 'hon. minister understand that I repudiated that? The very ground for my motion this morning was that there had been absolute breach of faith on the part of the Deputy Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Then, the hon. member for St. John was not speaking by the book when he invited us on this side to vote for the motion because it implied nothing more than that the Deputy Speaker had made a mistake. The motion simply declares that the action of the Deputy Speaker ' was a violation of the rules and constituted an infringement of the privileges of this House/ This is 'another startling instance of the 'perfect agreement' in which hon. members opposite are. The hon. member
for Pictou complains of a breach of faith, but the hon. member for St. John says that the motion implies nothing more than that the Deputy Speaker made a mistake in interpreting the rules.
As I was saying, this motion which was offered by the hon. member for St. John was sought to be made in absolute violation of the rules. It was not made during discussion, and though necessarily of the nature of an amendment, was made in the face of a rule which prohibited amendment. There was no interval in which it could be presented as a substantive motion. The motion had been made. At first the hon. gentleman said the question had not been put; now he says it had not been properly put. But that is immaterial. There was no interval in which the motion could be presented; the Deputy Speaker was proceeding to put the question. If there had been an interval of time it would have been simply due to interruptions, in direct and flagrant violation of the ruling of the Deputy Speaker, by hon. gentlemen on the other side seeking to make motions which they had no right to make and to prevent the proceedings going on. As a matter of reasonable and proper application of the rules it would not be an interval in the proceedings, even if these hon. gentlemen had, by these irregularities and violations of the rules, prevented the Deputy Speaker from getting a hearing to put the question. So, this could not be presented as a substantive motion, because there was no interval when it could be presented. That being so, it was the duty of the Deputy Speaker to proceed and have the question decided, notwithstanding the difficulties in his way. So, it seems to me, it is impossible to say that the action of the Deputy Speaker was in violation of the rules of the House. In no other way could he have carried out the rule, and he would have violated the rule if he had stopped to listen to hon. gentlemen opposite seeking to make propositions which must either have been for the purpose of initiating debate or for the purpose of proposing an amendment or motion in the nature of an amendment. For the rule told him that the question must be decided without debate and without amendment.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman consider that the Prime Minister was in order in making his motion in view of the fact that he had been speaking once before?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
One of two things is
true. Either the consideration of the clauses mentioned in the notice of motion had been concluded when the right hon. leader of the House made his motion or they had not been concluded. If they had been concluded, then for the reason which was invoked in support of the Tight of the hon.

member for Cape Breton South to make this motion, the right hon. Prime Minister had the right to make his motion.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: Might I suggest that the hon. member for Cape Breton South was speaking on a proposal to add a new clause to the Bill, but that was not the case with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:

I understood the hon. member for St. John to say that the Chairman had actually put his motion. I only refer to the matter to point out how hard pressed the hon. member was to find an argument when he had to try to rest one upon the slip made and immediately corrected by the Chairman by saying: The motion is that I do now rise-that I do report the Bill. in this particular instance. The Deputy Speaker's tongue slipped-
