speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I do not propose to
address myself to the argument which I had the misfortune not to hear this morning, but, as the hon. gentleman has seen fit to interrupt me for the purpose of making that affirmation, I do want to say that whether or not that affirmation is true does not depend on the argument that the hon. gentleman made this morning. That is an affirmation of fact, arid we ali sat here and we all saw and heard what took place. For my part, if 1 were in the position of the Deputy Speaker of this House, I would, so far as any imputation of bad faith is concerned, be perfectly ready to rest my case upon the events as they were seen and heard by every hon. gentleman sitting in this House. If I were in the position of the Deputy Speaker, I would be willing to find my compensation for the belief the hon. member for Pictou may entertain in the fact of my own consciousness, backed up by the opinion of the great majority of the witnesses of what took place, that there was absolutely no foundation for an imputation of that kind. The hon. member for St. John is not accustomed to setting aside points that may be injurious to an adversary when there is anything to be said in support of them, and yet he abandoned this imputation. I can only express my regret in view of what that hon. gentleman thought it proper to ssy in this House, that the hon. member for Pictou found it necessary to make that affirmation.

Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER:	I think all
the members of this House who were present this morning, on this side or the other side, will agree that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who has put in your hands, Mr. Speaker, the motion now before the House, presented his views in a fair, temperate, and moderate manner. I am sorry to say that the answer which was given to him was not, in my judgment, fair, temperate, or judicial. This is the more to be regretted because of the fact that the hon. gentleman who rose to answer the hon. member for Pictou was my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). I do the hon. member for Portage la Prairie the credit of saying that he is a very close and logical reasoner, and that his speeches are always replete with argument and free from invective. On this occasion, however, it was quite the reverse: his speech was replete with invective and barren of argument. But my hon. friend is a lawyer, and he remembered the old adage of the profession, ' if you have no case, abuse the plaintiff's attorney.' My hon. friend, in the opening sentences of his speech-I hope what I say will be without offence-reminded me of a well-known character in one of the works of Charles Dickens, the Artful Dodger, who picked a pocket in a bookstall and, in order to avoid discovery, raised the hue and cry ' stop thief,' thus diverting suspicion from himself and placing it upon poor Oliver Twist, who was an innocent spectator. The first word of my hon. friend was that if anybody was deserving of censure it was not the Deputy Speaker but the hon. member for Pictou himself and those associated with him on this side of the House. In this statement my hon. friend was following the course of the Artful Dodger, in trying to transfer the guilt, if guilt there be, from one side of the House to the other. I think we should discuss this matter in a temperate manner so as to come to a correct conclusion as to what are the rights of members on both sides of the House. The motion which we have to deal with is in these terms:
Resolved, that the action of Mr. Blondin, the Deputy Speaker, as Chairman of the Committee of the Whole House, while the committee was considering Bill No. 21, entitled, ' an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire,' in refusing to permit Mr. Carroll, the member for South Cape Breton, to move to add an additional section to said Bill, and also in declining to put the motion that the Chairman do now leave the Chair, as moved by Mr. Pugsley, the member for the city of St. John, was a violation of the rule3 and constituted an infringement of the privileges of this House.
Whether or not this motion is well founded, I think I can appeal to the members who were present last Friday; and, if their memory is defective, they may refresh it by referring to ' Hansard.' When the House met on Friday it took up almost immediately Bill No. 21, referred to in this motion, for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire. Immediately on the resumption in committee of the consideration of the Bill, my right hon. friend the leader of the Government moved the motion of which he had given notice the day before, which was in these terms:
That further consideration of the second, third, fourth and fifth sections and the proposed sixth section of this Bill shall he the first business of the committee and shall not be further postponed.
Shortly after the motion had been adopted and therefore had become the rule of the House for the time being, the hon. member for South Cape Breton moved the following motion:
That the following be added to the Bill as section 7:	,
Whenever practicable, in the construction of the ships provided under this Act, the contractors or builders shall be bound to accept steel and other materials produced in Canada at the current prices for the time being in Canada.
The point was taken that this motion could not be moved at that time after the original motion had been passed by the House, and undoubtedly, the point was well taken, because the House had just determined that clauses 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 should be the first business of the committee; and, of course, so long as those clauses had not been disposed of, no addition could be made to the Bill. This point was debated, and the Chairman addressing himself to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, then said:
I think it would be more advisable if the hon. .member would defer his motion until we have disposed of clause 6. There is an amendment and a sub-amendment to clause 3.
If that meant anything, it meant that the hon. member for South Cape Breton could not move his clause until we had disposed of clause 6 and that it would then be open to him to move the proposed clause 7 of which he had given notice.
In view of the discussion which has taken place this morning, it is well that I should call the attention of the House to the opinion which was expressed then and there by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie:
Mr. Meighen:	As a matter of order, I
would suggest to the hon. gentleman that there would be no difficulty about him making a motion immediately after the disposition of the two sub-amendments to clause 2 by way of an amendment and he can do the same with respect to the other clauses.



I beg to differ from the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. My hon. friend from Cape Breton could have moved his motion to any of the clauses of the Bill if it was germane to the subject of such clause.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
read my remarks slightly incorrectly. I said ' other clauses.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
-and he can do 'the same with respect of the other clauses.
I do not see the point. If he could do it with them all.

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: The significance of it is this, that immediately after the Chairman had suggested moving it after clause 6 had been disposed of, Mr. Carroll himself remarked that he desired to move it after clause 3. Some further remarks took place and I pointed out that it could be moved on clause 2 after the amendment had been disposed of and went on to say that it could be moved as an amendment to clause 3 when the amendment was disposed of.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend from Cape Breton had wanted to
make his motion as an amendment, he could have moved it on clause 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, if it had been germane to any of these clauses; but the point is that he did not choose to move an amendment; he had given notice of a new clause, to be clause 7, and there was good reason for it. I have the Bill before me. I doubt if the motion proposed to be made by my hon. friend from Cape Breton would have been germane to any clause. Clause 2 reads:
That further consideration of the second, third, fourth and fifth sections and the proposed sixth section of this Bill shall he the first business of the committee and shall not be further postponed.
I submit to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that the motion which the hon. member for Cape Breton wanted to move would not have been an amendment germane to this section. Neither would it have been germane to clause 4, which is as follows:
The said ships when constructed and equipped shall be placed by the Governor in Council at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of the Empire.
Nor would it have been germane to clause 5, which is as follows:
The said sum shall be paid, used and applied, and the said ships shall be constructed and placed at the disposal of His Majesty subject to such terms, conditions and arrangements as may be agreed upon between the Governor in Council and His Majesty's Government.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
Neither would it have been germane to clause 6, which I have not before me, but which, if I remember aright, provided simply for an accounting for the expenditure. As an amendment it might have been germane to clause 3; I did not say the the reverse. Clause 3 reads as follows:
The said sum shall be used and applied under the direction of the Governor in Council in the construction and equipment of battleships or armoured cruisers of the most modern and powerful type.
But if my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton did not choose to make it an amendment but a substantive clause, who could object to his doing so? He was within his rights. The point is that my hon. friend, having chosen to make his motion one for a substantive clause, clause 7, it could not be moved until clauses from 2 to 6 had been disposed of. As to that it seems'to me there can be no doubt. The motion of my hon. friend could not have been made pending the discussion of these clauses. Then the question arises, could it have been made after the others had been disposed of? I say there is no question that it could have been made. The only question at issue was whether it could have been made after two o'clock in the morning. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has expressed the opinion that no new clause could then be introduced; but I am sure the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie will agree that, if we had finished the consideration of clauses 2 or 6 before two o'clock in the morning, no objection could have been raised against my hon. friend moving his motion as clause 7. The only question is whether or not my hon. friend could have moved his motion after two o'clock in the morning. It was two o'clock in the morning when we finished the consideration of clauses 2 to 6. Then my hon. friend tried to move his motion, and the question arose, could he move iti after two o'clock in the morning? I must say in all fairness that the Prime Minister doubted, in fact, he affirmed that the motion could not be made after two o'clock in the morning. He said:
I might say to my hon. friend that he could move his amendment to clause 2 before two1 o'clock, but I do not think he could do so afterwards, and he could do it on the third reading if he desires to do so.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie did me the honour to quote my words and to say that I had approved this dictum of the Prime Minister. It is true that I spoke immediately after the Prime Minister had uttered the remarks that I ha we just quoted. 1 said:
That is the puzzle. He can not do it after two o'clock, but he can not do it before the clause is disposed of, and if it is not dis-,

posed of before two o'clock, be is shut off all-togeffher. You can do anything you please upi two o'clock, but after two o'clock the axe fails.	|
If my hon. friend thinks I said this in approval of what the Prime Minister had said, I am sorry to say that my power of expressing myself is not adequate to my thought. My hon. friend will find, at page 9811, a little colloquy between the Prime Minister and myself in which I expressed my thoughts:
Mr. Borden: My right hon. friend said in reply to that statement: 1 Then, everything is to be shut off at two o'clock.'
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Not according to the rule, but according to the will of my hon. friend.
Mr. Borden: According to the rule. I had risen, at the conclusion of the last vote, to move that the Bill be reported, and I had a perfect right to rise and make that motion.
It is so clear that I had no intention of saying that I approved of the interpretation put upon the rule [DOT] by the Prime Minister, that this motion could not be made after two o'clock, that when my hon. friend the member for South Cape Breton attempted to move his motion, I took the point of order that he had the right to move it, and we had a long discussion upon it. But the point of order which I raised was not disposed of by the Chairman, and it is still undecided. I made the best argument I could upon it; at ail events,
I think I made a case in favour of the proposition that, after the disposal of clauses 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, my hon. friend the member for South Cape Breton had a perfect right to move an addition to the Bill. The point of order was discussed at some length, when all of a sudden the Chairman interrupted the proceedings to rule upon another point of order. He decided then that the motion of my hon. friend from South Cape Breton could not be entertained, because he had risen after the Prime Minister. The ruling of the Chairman is to be found on page 9819 of ' Hansard,' and -is in these words:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
I was going to explain and to make clear to the committee how the question stood. Before this discussion is permitted to go on there is a question to be disposed of first by the Chairman on his responsibility, and that is the question of who had the floor. It has been said that the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) bad the floor, but it is for the Chairman tb decide. I must say that I saw the Prime Minister first.
It is quite possible that the Chairman saw the Prime Minister first; but, in face of the record, I maintain that if the Chairman saw the Prime Minister first, he gave the floor, not to the Prime Minister, but to the hon. member for South Cape Breton. The record is to be found in the pages of * 310i	. *[DOT]'ijfl
*	* Hansard.' On page 9809, after section 6 " had been agreed to, we find that the Prime J Minister rose and said:
Mr. Borden: I beg to move, Mr. Chairman, . that the Bill be reported as amended.
. Mr. Carroll:	This afternoon I intimated
*	that I proposed to make a motion adding an-r other clause to the Bill.
I claim that then and there the Chair-_ man gave the floor not to the Prime Minister, but to the hon member for South Cape Breton. How do I prove it? I prove it by the fact that at that moment, when the hon. i member for South Cape Breton had the floor, my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie rose to a point of order. The point of order was this:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Let the hon. member state his point of order. A point of order is always m order.
Mr. Meighen: My point of order is that the : i Minister having moved that we report this Bill an amendment cannot be moved.
If the point of order of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie was that the Prime Minister , having moved that we report the Bill no other amendment should be admitted, it was because the man who then had the floor was the hon. member against whom he moved, the hon. member for bouth Cape Breton. Therefore I conclude that, though it may be that the Chairman had seen the Prime Minister first, he had given a pledge to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, and, having given it, he could not take it from him afterwards. What is the reason that the Chairman gave the floor, not to the Prime Minister, but to the hon. member for South Cape Breton?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Does the right hon.
gentleman contend that because an hon. gentleman said a few words he was expressly given the floor by the Chairman ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
Yes, when
that hon. member, who has been speaking a few words and is interrupted by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, has the floor. If he had not the floor my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie would not have raised the point of order against him that he had no right to move his amendment.
It is quite intelligible why the Chairman saw the hon. member for South Cape Breton first, and not the Prime Minister. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie _ made a statement this morning with which I am disposed to agree. He stated that the first man in this House who had the right to be heard was the right hon. leader of the Government. I have no exception to take to that. He followed that up with the statement that the next man to be heard was the right hon. leader of the Opposition. I agree with that also. But

then my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie thought that there might be reasons, conditions, or circumstances, in which the floor could be given, not to the leader of the Opposition, but to another hon. member. And there may be circumstances-I think I use exactly the language of my hon. friend -in which the floor can be taken away from the leader of the Opposition. Indeed, that has happened before in this very House, and during this very session. But let that pass. I ask my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, if there are circumstances in which the floor can be taken from the leader of the Opposition, are there not circumstances in which the floor can be taken from the Prime Minister?

maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext: I pointed out clearly that the responsibility would be taken by the House, and not by Mr. Speaker, or by the Chairman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MR. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
But before the House decides the Speaker or the Chairman has to decide. My hon. friend said very truly to-day that the Speaker or the Chairman is the arbiter; it is for him to decide. He can give the floor to any one he sees first. He ought to see the Prime Minister first, and he ought to see the leader of the Opposition next; and, if there are circumstances in which the floor can be taken from either the one or the other, that can be decided. What was the reason why on the present occasion the floor should have been taken away from the Prime Minister and given to the hon. member for South Cape Breton? There has been a good deal of disquisition and special pleading in this House, but there are certain rules which appeal to every man of intelligence and fairness, and which are understood even by those who are not familiar with all the rules. This was the case. Earlier in the day, when my hon. friend from South Cape Breton had moved his amendment, the Chairman had told him this:
I cannot hear you now; I think it would be more advisable if the hon. member would defer his motion until we have disposed of clause 6.
He remembered that. When clause 6 had been disposed of, the hon. member for South Capee Breton rose, the Prime Minister also rose, and the Chairman gave the floor to the hon. member for South Cape Breton. Why? Because he had given his word to the hon. member that he would hear him. That was the reason, I suppose, why he saw the hon. member for South Cape Breton, and not the Prime Minister.
Now, Sir, I submit, in all fairness, that this is an assembly in which the word of a member ought to be his bond. When the Chairman had said to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, I will hear you later when we have
Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
disposed of clause 6, he might well have said to the Prime Minister: It is true that you have the right to be heard first in this House, but I told the hon. member for South Cape Breton earlier in the day that I would hear him, and I will hear him now. That is the point. But the Chairman of the committee, after having given the floor to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, gave it to the Prime Minister. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice did not know how it was that the Chairman had violated the privileges of the House. Here is an instance. After having given a promise to the hon. member for South Cape Breton that he would give him an opportunity to be heard, when the time came to fulfil his pledge, and to hear the hon. member for South Cape Breton, he would not hear him, but, on the contrary, said that he would hear the Prime Minister first.
I can go beyond all these technicalities;
I appeal to the fairness of every gentleman in this House, and I ask, why was not the hon. member for South Cape Breton given the floor and allowed to make his motion? It has been said that the Prime Minister could rise after two o'clock. I do not deny it. But if the Prime Minister could rise after two o'clock, every other member of this House could also do so; and if no member of this House could rise after two o'clock, then the Prime^ Mini^tei had no right to be allowed to rise. The Prime Minister, after all, is only a member of this House, so far as obedience to the rules is concerned, and has no more privilege on the floor of this House than the humblest member on either side. It is said by hon. gentlemen opposite that the hon. member for South Cape Breton had not the right to make this motion. For the purposes of the argument let that be admitted; but at all events the hon. member for South Cape Breton thought he had the right to make the motion, and the duty of the Chairman was to point out to him that he could not make the motion and could net speak because it was after two o'clock. But the Chairman did not do that, and for that reason alone he is liable to the censure of the House.	.
I now pass to the action of the Chairman in refusing to put the motion of the hon member for St. John. There has been a good deal of special pleading on the part of the Minister of Justice on this point; but the question is a very simple one, and all the ingenuity of the Minister of Justice will not convince anybody that the plain English language cannot be understood even by the simplest member of this House. The Minister of Justice has made a long disquisition as to what is the meaning of the motion that the Chairman leave the Chair. Here is the plain letter of the law. and I appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. MAY 13, 1913
Meighen), who understands these matters, if it is not s >;
Rule 15. A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair is always in order.
That is not a motion in amendment; it is a motion in interruption of the proceedings of the House. This very day the Prime Minister said that if that motion had passed it would kill the Bill, which is true, and the Bill would have disappeared from the Order Paper for the time being. I have made myself

I made no further attempt to move my motion. As a matter of fact, sections 2, 3, 4 and 5 were not finished until after two o'clock in the morning. Immediately after section 6 was finished, I rose in my place, and I want to say here, and there is no hon. member who knows it better than the hon. member for Portage la Prai rie, that when I rose in my place and the hon. leader of the Government rose at the same time, the Deputy Speaker never saw the Prime Minister, he turned absolutely around and recognized me, and the right hon. Prime Minister took his seat. I want to say further that, until the hon. member for Portage la Prairie called the attention of the Deputy Speaker, that hon. gentleman did not know that the Prime Minister was on his feet. Now, I want to make myself plain and thoroughly understood. I took it for granted, as I think any hon. member would have taken it for granted, that I should have the right, after clause .6 was disposed of, to make the motion which I had been ready to make when the House met at three o'clock in the afternoon. My hon. friend from North Grey said: Whom would the Chairman be likely to notice first, for whom would he likely have his eye open? I say that in this particular instance he had his eye open for the man who was supposed to move that motion, and whom he had given to understand in the evening had a perfect right to move that motion. And I believe as I say with all confidence, that the Deputy Speaker did notice me risins in my nlace

and did not notice the Prime Minister. And there is no member who knows it better than the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. ' Hansard ' is not very complete on this matter. I am making no objection on that score. ' Hansard ' does not contain all the remarks I made on that night on rising. I do not want to impute any motives; I do not want to say it was done for a purpose-I do not see what purpose it would serve-but I say I was speaking at least one minute before the hon. member for Portage la Prairie rose to speak at all. And, it was well understood in the afternoon that I was to have the floor, I think that the Deputy Speaker recognized me and understood that I should have had the floor. And I think that instead of this resolution being brought against the Deputy Speaker, it should be brought against certain other hon. gentlemen in this House for having misled him.
Coming to the motion that was made by the hon. member for St. John, it is contended on the other side of the House that that motion was out of order. I may say that if that motion was out of order, the Deputy Speaker did not then take the proper course. Under rule 44 of this House it is provided:
Whenever the Speaker is of opinion that a motion offered to the House is contrary ito the roles and privileges of Parliament, he shall apprise the House thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the rule or authority applicable to the case.
What does Bourinot say about that?
If a motion be out of order, the Speaker! will call attention to the irregularity, and1 refuse to put it to the House under the thirty-second rule.
Which i3 now rule 44. Why did not the Chairman take that course? Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House talk of courtesy. While we appreciate courtesy on this side of the House, we more truly appreciate the free exercise of our rights, and it was not only the right but the duty of the Deputy Speaker on that occasion to inform the hon. member for St. John of the fact that he was out of order, instead of ignoring him as he did. His motion was either in order or it wa3 out of order. If it was in order, the Chairman should have put it; if it was out of order, the Chairman should have proceeded, under rule 44, to give his reasons why that motion was not in order. I do not exactly appreciate the distinction which the hon. Minister of Justice was trying to draw between rules 39 and 15 of this House. I doubt very much if he knew it himself when he concluded his remarks. Buie 15 of the House is so framed that the ordinary man would clearly understand it, and I take it for granted that the Minister of Justice who occupies Mr. CARROLL.
such a prominent position in this country, would have no trouble in grasping its meaning. He told us during the course of his remarks that we should read the rules precisely in the language in which they are couched, but afterwards, when he was met by rule 15, he could not read it according to its wording and at the same time give to it the interpretation which he desired to give. Rule 15 is as follows:
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chairi is always in order, and shall take precedence of any other motion.
I do not know that any hon. gentleman of this House could make that rule any plainer than it i3. Then the right hon. Prime Minister said that the hon. member for St. John was not in possession of the House when he made this motion. Most assuredly he was not in possession of the House when he made the motion, and that is the very reason why this motion of censure is offered. He should have put the hon. member for St. John in possession of the House. A member is not in possession of the House until he has made a motion and that motion has been recognized by the Chair. There was, therefore, no possible way in which the hon. member for St. John could have put himself in possession of the House other than by moving, as he did, that the Chairman leave the Chair. It is rather difficult to say what constitutes the catching of the eye of the Chairman or the Speaker in this House at the present time. I always understood, when the Chairman in any deliberative body turned around and listened to the speaker for almost a minute, that that was pretty nearly catching the eye of the Chairman. But that is not catching the eye of the Chairman at all. There is always some difficulty in this House in catching the eye of the Chairman or the Speaker, especially if a number of hon. gentlemen wish to speak, but it strikes me that when it comes to the catching of the illusive reversible eye of a Nationalist-Tory Deputy Speaker by an English-speaking member of this House, the difficulty is almost insurmountable.
I desire to say that in any remarks that I have made in connection with this matter I am not guided by any animus, but solely by the feeling that the rules of this House should be properly interpreted. I do say, however, that it is rather annoying, and that it runs against the grain, when we find that hon. gentlemen who are placed in a position of trust in this House do not give to those rules that fair interpretation which the English language places upon them.

speechtext:
I do not think I
would have troubled the House with any additional remarks upon this subject were it not for the fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice seemed to be painfully

shocked because I reiterated a statement
which I made earlier in the day, that this resolution involved a charge of bad faith on the part of the Deputy Speaker in his conduct during the sitting on Friday last. The attitude which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice adopts when any member of this House ventures to say anything about anybody who belongs to his particular flock is becoming one of the most amusing things of this session; and it is a role which the hon. gentleman assumes with very great ability. If any gentleman on this side in the course of a debate attempts to-say anything even less suggestive than the circumstances actually warrant, the Minister of Justice always rushes into the breach, pounces upon this little morsel and magnifies it into a very large and important consideration. . I regret very much that the hon. minister is not present, that 1 might make clear to him-and this I think I made reasonably clear to hon. members of .this House in opening the discussion this morning-what my view was in bringing this motion to the attention of the House. Sir, I did not offer this motion for amusement; I did not move it as a bit of child's-play. I was in the House on Friday evening arid Saturday morning when the Deputy Speaker was presiding over the deliberations of the committee. I saw what transpired; I knew that he had done what he had no right to do, and hence I have offered this motion and ask the House to vote upon it. Why should hon. gentlemen of this House, when they see the rules violated and their privileges taken away, hesitate to express their views in regard to the matter? So far as I am concerned, I do not hesitate to do so. What are the facts in regard to this matter? The Deputy Speaker, the Chairman of committees of this House, gave the word to my hon. friend the member for South Cape Breton on Friday afternoon that, after all the clauses of the Bill were disposed of he would have the right to move the amendment which he mentioned to the committee at that time. Everyody knows, that if we weed out all the discussion, the metaphysical, hairsplitting performances of the hon. member *for Portage la Prairie and the other gentlemen who tried to decloud the issue, that *assurance was given in the afternoon and we have the word of the hon. member for Cape Breton that, relying upon the word of the Deputy Speaker, he rose, understanding that he had recognition from the Deputy Speaker, and proposed to make his amendment in accordance with the understanding and that he was prevented from doing so because the Deputy Speaker did hot allow him. With that state of facts, what is the House going to do? As my right hon. leader pointed out there will be other Speakers here in other days. Do hon. gentlemen opposite wiant that to be the method and the permanent rule of this House in
dealing with committees, are they prepared, simply because they happen to sit on the treasury benches, to adopt such rules, which are to go on record in the Journals of the House, and may hereafter be invoked against them? If they are, then the blood will be on their own heads. But methods of that character are subversive of parliamentary government and of British institutions in this country and when hon. gentlemen attempt to utilize these methods in order to pass legislation which is supposed to be the product of those who are the special guardians of everything that means standing for British institutions, then they and their legislation become a farce in this free country ;and the people are recognizing that fact. What more, Sir? It has been shown by my right hon. leader, in the statement which he made a few moments ago, that the Deputy Speaker deliberately disregarded the point of order raised by my hon. friend from Beauce and the motion which my hon. friend from St. John had a right to inaKe, 'disregarded both df those gentlemen when they had the floor and were addressing him, pointing out to him for his consideration a point of order and a motion which, under the rule, he wa.s bound to deal with. Why did he not put them to the House? Why did he not consider them? Either he was rattled and did not know what he was doing or he was doing it deliberately, there can be only one of two situations. The right hon. the Prime Minister recognized that fact when he pleadingly told us that the hon. gentleman, the Deputy Speaker, had had a great many trying experiences this session, an apologetic way of trying to let the hon. gentleman down. Parliament should not have men in the presiding seats who lose their heads and if such men are put in those seats, the Government and the political party that put them there should take them out and put in men who keep their heads on in those cases. The Prime Minister to-day did not venture, as some of the lesser lights behind him did, to argue that the hon. member for Cape Breton had no right to make the motion; on the contrary, he iterated and reiterated the proposition that the hon. member for South Cape Breton could have got his amendment presented to the House on three other different occasions. Because the hon. member for South Cape Breton could have moved his amendment on three other different occasions, therefore the Deputy Speaker was justified in illegally preventing him from moving it at the time when he did want to move it properly. On section 4-dates of sessions:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Bill stood over the other day for further consideration of the third paragraph of section 32 in the Act, as set forth in clause 4 of the present Bill. That clause provides:
The dates in the preceding subsection, fixed for the beginning of each session, may be varied by the Governor in Council, or by the court, provided that notice shall be given ini the Canada Gazette not less than four weeks before the date which may be fixed for the beginning of any session.

When the Bill was before the committee previously, the right hon. the leader of the Opposition urged against the adoption of this clause, the consideration that in operation it might prove inconvenient to members of the profession engaged before that court. The objection struck me at the time as having considerable force, and, as I have said, the Bill stood over in order to give it further consideration. I have given the matter that further consideration, and I would like to call attention to two points in that regard. I have pointed out that this power conferred upon the court or upon the Governor in Council would be exercised only for grave reasons. I might mention a reason which did not occur to me the other day why it is desirable that this power should be made susceptible of being exercised, and I believe that reason is of sufficient weight to perhaps over-ride the objection offered. At present the dates of the opening of the different terms are fixed and the provision is that the term shall continue until the business before the court has been disposed of, which is to say until the cases before the court have been heard. It has been pointed out to me that it works out in this way: that at a particular term there may lie a much larger number of cases than usual, with the result that the date of the next following term being absolutely fixed, the justices are unable to dispose of the cases heard at one term before they are obliged to begin the hearing of cases in the next term. It is very desirable in the interests of the proper administration of justice that wherever it is possible the cases heard in one term should be disposed of before the justices are called upon to sit in another term and take new oases. It has been pointed out that the last term of the court was unusually prolonged, and that if by reason of the court having to begin at the date fixed it has not disposed of the cases heard in that term, the probability is that some of the cases would necessarily be carried over the long vacation. The objection was urged that this provision might prove of great inconvenience to barristers practising before the court if there was no absolute certainty as to the date of the commencement of the term. I think we can 'trust the court not to exercise this power without grave reason, even though the power be confided in them. This Bill has been some little time before the House, and while I am not in a position to say that it has been communicated to members of the Bar, it is a fact that I have had communications from leading members of the profession endorsing certain of its provisions, and [DOT]there has been no suggestion of objection to this.
Mr. DOHERTY.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I cannot say
that I have been convinced by the reasons advanced by the Minister of Justice, but in a matter of this kind I shall have to give way to his opinion. If I understood the minister aright, he stated that the calendar for a certain term may be so charged that that term would actually overlap the next term. That, of course, must be a very rare occurrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is possible, but I am willing to admit it is very improbable. What I said was, that in one instance the term had been so prolonged and such a large number of cases had been heard that the interval between that and the date fixed for the next term was not sufficiently long to enable the judges to adjudicate upon and dispose of all the eases heard in the preceding term. That, of course, would create considerable delay in the decision of cases, because the judges would be obliged to abandon the consideration of the cases already heard and enter upQn the hearing of new cases. It is in the interests of_ the public that every facility should he given for having cases adjudicated upon as promptly as possible after they have been heard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is that the
only reason why cases are protracted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
say that is the only reason, but the smaller the number of reasons for protracting cases the better for all concerned.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the h"on. Minister of Justice will allow me to make a few observations on what he has just said. It is certain that the hon. judges-I speak especially for the Bar of the province of Quebec-are overburdened with work; that they have too many cases to adjudicate upon and dispose of. When a term is concluded, another one begins almost immediately after, and,they have not the time to give the necessary attention to the cases already heard.
I agree entirely with what has just declared the hon. minister. But there is another reason, which is that since many years we are vainly asking for a greater number of judges. It is certain that such a state of things works to the detriment of judiciary business, especially in Montreal. We have asked, and we keep constantly asking, since many years, for more judges, as we also ask for them a higher salary; and nothing is done.
The hon. minister, who knows better than any one the state of things to which I refer, because he has practised during a long while in Montreal, where he has also administered justice as a judge, knows that what I say is true. We are on the

verge of a revolt in Montreal, and requests upon requests, petitions upon petitions, follow in an uninterrupted flow towards the. Government, but all that to no avail.
In the present moment, we are obliged to ask judges from the surrounding districts to come to Montreal, so as to aid in the administration of justice.
Lately, I was present at the general meeting of the Bar, and many bitter complaints have been heard about that state of things. The question is heard on all sides: "Why is the Minister of Justice remaining inactive."
There are certainly many lawyers who will feel honored in being called to the Bench. Many members would also esteem that a great favour, if they can decently get away from politics. Is the Government afraid to open up another county?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We might, for instance, open up the county of Montcalm.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Justice may open this county, where I stand ready to meet him.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We do not usually call millionaires to the Bench.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Grand Master of the Nationalists came there once with the intention to defeat me, but he had to go away as he came, that is, all his plans came to nought.
The Montreal Bar is clamouring for new judges, and if you do not accede to those wishes you are not giving justice to the Province of Quebec. Business has considerably increased. From a judiciary point of view, the importance of Montreal has now grown to be much more considerable than is generally imagined. We have to wait four or five days before our cases can be heard. Last Friday I was in Montreal to attend to a case which had been entered for that day, and it was only this morning that I have been able to get a hearing.
The Bar of the province of Quebec is the only one of which so little account is taken.
I would like to see the Ontario Bar in the same situation. There would be such a hubbub, that force would be to listen to that grievance. But, for the Quebec Bar, everything is good enough.
I am asking, for the sake of justice, to put an end to such a state of things. Before long, the Minister of Justice will have a deputation of the Bar of Montreal [DOT]call upon him. I have told them the other day: Go to Ottawa, and compel the minister to hear your grievances; set things on fire, if it is necessary . . . Business men go to Ottawa; you must do the same thing; call upon the Minister of Justice, and wake him up, and stir him up.
I am also asking for an increase of salary for judges, because that is absolutely
necessary for the proper administration of justice; as I have been asking since a long while for an increase of the indemnity of the deputation, and you are not doing anything. And you call that rendering justice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that we are now discussing a Bill which concerns the Supreme Court.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: However, I hope the hon. Minister of Justice will take in good part my remarks, and that he will see about remedying the evil we are complaining of.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I do not know that there are so many entreaties, as is stated by my hon. friend, made with the object of increasing the number of judges, at all events as regards the Superior Court. I must say to my hon. friend that, so far as I know, the department has not been petitioned to incease the number of judges.
Moreover, I must draw his attention to the fact that it depends neither on myself, nor on the Government, nor on the Parliament, to take the necessary steps to increase the number of judges; that power lies exclusively in the Legislature of the Province of Quebec; to that Legislature alone belongs the right to ask for an increase in the number of the judges of the Superior Court. That Legislature has already provided for the nomination of three supplementary judges for the Circuit Court, and the hon. member, if I understand the situation, has no cause for complaint as regards the number of judges of that Court, because three judges of the Superior Court have helped the judges of the Circuit Court for the dispatch of judiciary business.
As regards the increase of the number of judges of which he has spoken, I hope to be able, in a couple of days, to tell him what decision the Government has taken on the matter.
In concluding I am happy to see that the hon. member for Montcalm is supporting the Government as regards the question now before this Committee.
Oh section 5-amount in dispute:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I move:
That section 5 be amended by adding at the end of section the words, ' by affidavit or affidavits.'
The section provides that proof may be made in cases where the value of the matter in controversy does not appear on the face of the record. It seemed to me desirable that we should indicate a method whereby that value can be proved.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Has the hon. minister
considered the question of appeals from the Supreme Court of Canada to the Judicial

r?:i
Committee of the Privy Council? There is a very strong feeling in Canada that our Supreme Court should be the final court of appeal. After a case has appeared before a trial judge, a divisional court, a court of appeal in a province and has then reached the Supreme Court of the Dominion of Canada, all the law in connection with such a case should be thoroughly known and its value fully considered and digested. I think it should be finally decided there. I quite appreciate the fact that the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is, without exception, the grandest tribunal in the world. I had some experience before the Judicial Committee. As constituted, it is composed of the best intellect that Great Britain can produce. Notwithstanding that fact, I think that we have sufficient legal ability in Canada to decide our own cases, and litigants in Canada should not be, in the final result, forced to go to the Judicial Committee, because that means an enormous expense beyond the capabilities of a very large number of litigants. It means that the wealthy litigant can probably win out against the poor one, because the latter cannot afford to pay the necessary fees. The Minister of Justice and the Government would do weir to consider this question carefully. Surely, if the United States Government can have their final court of appeal in their own country, we should be capable of having our final court of appeal in Canada.
The best judges obtainable should be appointed and paid salaries commensurate with their position. As a matter of fact, at the present time judges in this country are not paid salaries equal to what even a mediocre lawyer can earn. How can you expect to get the best legal talent on the Bench unless you pay salaries in accordance with their ability? Our revenues are big enough to justify the employment of the best legal talent in Canada, and to make the Supreme Court the final court of appeal. I ask the hon. the Minister of Justice and his colleagues to see if they cannot bring in a Bill to accomplish that purpose.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If I were speaking only for the province which I represent, with some sixty-four other members in this House, I would say: let us maintain as regards our province the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, because we have found, in that very high tribunal, justice and a respect for our laws and the precedents which have been created by a long series of judgments in our judicial world. I speak, however, as a Canadian; and I am bound to say that efforts, which are being made and which have been made for many years past, the Imperial Federation movement, will at some future time create, by reaction in this country, such a sentiment as the one which was Mr. GERMAN.
created in Australia at the time of the framing of the constitution of the Commonwealth, when Mr. Chamberlain and the British authorities had to strain everything in order to secure one class of appeals from Australia, namely, in constitutional cases. I am very frank in this matter. If I spoke as one coming from the province of Quebec, I should stand for the appeal to the Privy Council, because our code of laws in the province of Quebec has been, generally speaking, interpreted in a most satisfactory manner by the lords of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. But I say that this idea of trying to standardize everything or to model everything on the London pattern creates in the Dominion, by way of reaction, a sentiment quite contrary to that contemplated. My hon. friends will know by reading the reports of the various Imperial conferences that efforts have been made to create one appellate court for the Empire. There has been strong resistance offered to that movement, and the project has failed so far. I do not know what are the purposes of the legislation introduced of late by Lord Haldane, although the hon. Minister of Justice the other day gave the House a short synopsis of that legislation. I hope the hon. gentleman will find opportunity to give a fuller explanation. But there is a feeling in the country that attempts are being made to create in that way one appellate tribunal ior the Empire. It is a beautiful dream, but I do not think it can be realized. My hon. friend from Welland has said that the appeals should be restricted, that the number of higher courts was, so to speak, an invitation to litigants, and especially to wealthy litigants, to go to such higher courts at the expense of the poorer litigants. There is some truth in that. But I do not forget that any subject of His Majesty the King has what we call in French, ' l'appel de droit et 1'appel de grace.' Even the poorer and humbler among His Majesty's subjects have the right to appeal to the foot of the Throne. That is one of the safeguards which we at least, who belong to the minority, highly appreciate. I cannot emphasize too much what I stated at the beginning of my remarks, that in our relations with the Mother Country, when everything goes well, it is a good, safe principle to let well enough alone and not to attempt unrealizable schemes such as the creation of one Court of Apnea! for the whole of the Empire. The whole of the British fabric is elastic and adaptable to circumstances. In the Privy Council- I was there myself when I was Solicitor General-I have listened to cases from India, from British Guiana, from Ontario, from Quebec. You have interpreted there the common law of England; the civil code of the province of Quebec; the Dutch

law; the law of Scotland, which differs materially from the common law of England; you have the Roman law; you have the law of the Channel Islands, which is the old Norman law. And the judges hear the cases and listen to the counsel, and I have yet to learn that anybody has had to criticise the reports of the law lords to His Majesty. It is the best safeguard of the British citizenship for any of the subjects of His Majesty the King in any of the colonies or dominions. Therefore, any proposed change is to my mind not desirable, and if too much insistence is put upon it, if the idea of the creation of that unique tribunal for the British Empire is advocated, there will be a reaction in the Dominion. The reaction will not come in my province; it will come in Ontario, as it has already come; it will come in New Brunswick and the other English-speaking provinces. It is as well to let Imperial statesmen know that ' Let well enough alone ' is safe not only when it is used to defeat reciprocity, but even in our relations with the Mother Country from a judicial point of view.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
What I am going to say 1 say simply from the standpoint of a private member of this House, and I base it on my experience as a member of the Bar of New Brunswick. I do not quite appreciate the force of the argument advanced by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), for I see no connection whatever between the question of Imperial federation and the question of appeal by anyone in Canada to the judicial committee of the Privy Council. That appeal is a right we have had not only since Confederation but ever since we had courts in Canada, and to my mind it would be a great misfortune and a great mistake if the right of appeal to the Privy Council should be taken away and final appeals should be to the Supreme Court of Canada. I think the hon. member for Rouville struck the keynote when he said it was the right of any subject to carry his complaint to the fact of the Throne. The courts to which we go with our appeals is named a committee. In the olden times a petition was taken to the King who heard it in council. As time went on, that, of course, became unworkable, and so a Committee of the Privy Council was appointed consisting of men who are most eminent jurists, well trained and learned in the law who now hear these different appeals. I think it is one of the greatest safeguards which any minority or any poor man has in this country that if justice is not done by the courts of this country, they or he can go to a tribunal across the water entirely removed from any local .consideration, as litigants might
think the courts in this country are not removed, and get a decision on the merits of the case.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How can the poor man get there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look over the records of appeals to the Privy Council that have gone from Canada, I think he will find that there have been more decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council against the wealthy corporations and large interests than against the individuals who may have been fighting these corporations.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: H^w is the poor man to get to the Committee of the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I might ask the hon. gentleman how the poor man is to get to the Supreme Court of Canada?

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: He is in his own country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the cost of an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada is not inconsiderable. The main who appeals to the court and sustains defeat surely ought to have the right, if he is able to do so, to carry an appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which, as I understand, is entirely removed from any local or sectional considerations, and to which there may be imputed no consideration which mijght, perhaps very unjustly, be imputed to the courts of our own country. My hon. friend knows that if a litigant in this country takes an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, he can not then take an appeal to the Privy Council except by obtaining what is called special leave. Before taking a further appeal to the highest appellate court in the land, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, he has to apply fot leave to appeal, and has to show some reason why the appeal should be granted. As a matter of fact, that appeal will not be granted unless the case is one in which there is involved an important constitutional question or some important matter with regard to public policy. So that if an individual, carrying on litigation with a large company, has a judgment in his favour from a court in the province from which he comes, and that company takes an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and is defeated in that appeal, they cannot take a further appeal to the Privy Council without obtaining special leave, and this leave can only be obtained by showing special reason why some important or constitutional point should be adjudicated upon.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Supposing a poor man gets a judgment against him in the

Supreme Court of Canada after having had a judgment in his favour in the court below, where can he go?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That depends largely upon the means of the individual. I know cases in my own province, as, for instance, under the Employes' Liability for Injuries Act, under which there is no appeal from the decision of the judge, provided the plaintiff is willing to take proceedings under the provisions of the Act and not at common law. But, all things *considered, I think it would be a very great misfortune for this country if we were to abolish the right to appeal to [DOT]the Privy Council. We all know that although the judges of our courts in Canada are, in most cases, learned, fair-minded and honourable gentlemen, they have occupied various positions in the political and public life of the country, and whether rightly or wrongly, there are litigants who will think, perhaps without good reason, that the judgments given against them have been to some extent unconsciously influenced by tho views held by the judges .when they were in public life, or when they were associated with either of the political parties of the country. I think, under these circumstances, that it is a great privilege for them to have an opportunity of carrying their appeals from the Supreme 'Court- in Canada to the Privy Council in order that they may be adjudicated upon there-and as a rule the judgments of the Privy Council have met with approval in this country. My own experience as a member of the bar leads me to favour strongly the maintenance of the right to appeal to the Privy Council. I think that is the feeling of most of the members of the bar in Canada, and I believe that, if the matter were fairly discussed before the people of the country they would deem it to be a very great mistake if we were by legislation to take away the right that has always existed for any person in Canada to carry an appeal to the Privy Council and get a decision from that body, appointed by His Majesty the King and his advisors in the Cabinet of Great Britain. Whether or not we could take away that right is another matter; I presume it could be done by making a change in the British North America Act, and receiving the sanction oi the Imperial Parliament. I have no doubt that if this Parliament were desirous of making such a change, the Imperial Government would not stand in the way, if it ' were the desire of the Canadian people that the change should be made, subject of course to the exercise of the Royal prerogative. However, so far as the rights of minorities are concerned, and so far as the rights of every citizen of Canada are concerned, I would very much regret the taking of any step which Mr. GERMAN.
would result in abolishing the right to carry an appeal to the Privy Council, which has been established for the purpose of hearing appeals from the courts of the colonial possessions and overseas dominions of His Majesty. The right to carry his appeal to the foot of the throne is one of the great safeguards of the liberty of every British subject.
Mr. LAFORTUNE; I have listened with much interest to what the hon. Minister of Marine has said, and also the hon. member who preceded him. I have now thirty years' experience in the Bar, and I fully concur in what the hon. member for Welland has just said.
When the Supreme 'Court was established, I well remember the discussion which then took place, and I may say that the Court was created in view of abolishing the appeal to the Privy Council. That question of appeal to the Privy Council was seriously discussed at the time, and the 'Supreme Court was established with the object of doing away with that appeal.
At the present time, claims of three or four thousand dollars are reduced to one hundred and ninety-nine dollars so as to prevent the powerful companies against which an appeal is entered to go before the Privy Council. When a case has been heard by the judges of the Superior- Court, and has passed through the Court of Revision and the Court of Appeal, and then, afterwards, goes before the Supreme Court, who will say that such a case has not been then sufficiently discussed?
I must say, of that appeal to the Privy Council, that the remedy is worse than the evil. W'hen a powerful company has lost a case before our courts, it goes to England and enters an appeal before the Privy Council. Very often, that company goes there alone, because its opponent has not the necessary funds to push the case any further before that high jurisdiction, and the appeal is generally allowed in such case, because the discussion is not contradictory. A poor man has not the means to exhaust all the jurisdictions, and he is not always ready, as the powerful companies are, to cross the ocean in order to sustain his contention. It is open to him, it is true, to do so, but he has not the means to do it. I think that our laws and customs are much better interpreted by our own judges, than they could be by foreign judges.
Many jurists object to being called to the Bench, because the salary offered is not sufficient. It even happens that judges will sometimes leave the Bench because the salary is not high enough. Let us pay good salaries and choose the best men; we will have these competent Judges and our laws will be well interpreted. It will then be no longer necessary to cross the ocean.

It is always the question of salary which predominates; in other terms, if we expect to have good services we must pay for them. A country should find the means to compensate properly for services rendered. A few days ago, a salary of $12,500 was voted for an engineer, in the civil service. Must it he said that we deem matter to be more important than intelligence, since we hesitate so much in giving a proper remuneration to our judges. Let us make a choice among our best jurists, and we will have competent judges.
We hear that because a man has been mixed up with politics, his impartiality must be in question. Are we prepared to say that those men have mo conscience? When a man is called to the Bench and becomes a judge, he is there no longer a politician and his conscience becomes his sole guidance.
The remarks made by the hon. member for Welland are perfectly fair and I concur in everything he says. Is it not singular that we should see fit to appeal to some British Lords for the proper interpretation of our customs, of our laws, and our contracts passed between people of our country? I have the greatest admiration for those noble Lords, but, nevertheless, I must say that I have more respect for the judges who live in our midst, and who are acquainted with our usages, our laws and our customs. I prefer to be judged by men who have always lived among us rather than by those hon. gentlemen who live in far-away England.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
member for Welland in regard to civil cases though I think the case of appeal in constitutional cases should be preserved. The right of appeal in ordinary cases has been restricted in Australia, I think there are only constitutional cases going from the courts of Australia to the Privy Council. It is a very heavy expense for a litigant to go before the Privy Council. He has to commence by putting up security for costs. In Quebec I think the security is $2,000. I am not sure what it is in Ontario but I think it is $1,000. That is only the preliminary. Then the litigant has to supply his counsel with funds to make the trip and when the counsel gets across he generally employs another counsel to speak before the Privy Council. I do not suppose that we could pass any legislation here to restrict the right of appeal, because any subject of His Majesty has the right to go to the foot of the Throne. If such legislation was passed, I suppose it w'ould have to be passed by the Imperial Parliament, but this Parliament could petition the Imperial Parliament to pass legislation with respect to the right of appeal in ordinary cases and to preserve it only in constitutional
cases. In criminal cases there is no appeal from the Court of Appeal of the province to the Supreme Court unless there is a disagreement in the Court of Appeal and there is no appeal to the Privy Council unless there has been disagreement among the judges of the Supreme Court. If a subject has less facility to appeal to the Privy Council in a criminal case I do not see why he should have more facility to appeal In a case of ordinary civil rights. I am in favour of retaining the right of appeal only in constitutional cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Welland (Mr. German) has raised a question that affords a very large field for interesting discussion and we have had some such discussion. I would like to point out a couple of things. In the first place, under the law as at present, there is no right of appeal from the judgment of the Supreme Court to the Privy Council. The provision is that there shall be no appeal to any *court constituted by the Imperial Parliament saving only any prerogative right of His Majesty. The wording is:
Saving any Tight which His _ Majesty may be graciously pleased to exercise by virtue of his royal prerogative.
So that, so far as our law is concerned, there is no appeal to the Privy Council as a matter of right from the judgment of the Supreme Court. The Act simply-

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There should be no
special leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There would arise in that, connection very grave questions for consideration. There is the question in the first place could we interfere with any right, His Majesty, in virtue of his prerogative, may be able to exercise, and in the second place, if we could do that, would it be advisable for us to undertake to do it? That matter was very seriously discussed at the time the Act itself was passed and the final result was as I have indicated. The second thing I would like to point out to relieve the apprehension of the hon. member for Rouville of the danger of our being subjected to a right of appeal to some court that may be established in Great Britain, is that our Act has expressly excluded any appeal of that kind to any court that might be constituted in the future; by the provisions of our^ Act such a court is excluded from exercising jurisdiction. The wording of the Act is:
The judgment of the court shall in all cases be final and conclusive and no appeal shall be brought from any judgment or order of the court to any court of appeal established by the Parliament of Great Britain and Ireland by which appeals or petitions to His Majesty in Council may be ordered to be heard; saving any right which His Majesty



may be graciously pleased to exercise by virtue of his Royal prerogative.
So that so far as any court which the Parliament of Great Britain and Ireland might constitute, we have now express provision on that there shall be no appeal to it and it would require legislation of the Parliament of Canada to grant such an appeal from the judgment of the Supreme Court. It is not in our power to abolish the right of appeal to His Majesty in his Privy Council in regard to appeals from provincial courts. We are in a position to say, and we have said that, saving his Majesty's prerogative, there shall be no appeal from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada because we created that court and we have the right to determine the effect of its creation. But before there was any Supreme Court or any dominion there was a right of appeal from the final courts of appeal of a province to his Majesty in Council and that is a right of appeal, not a mere matter of going and asking leave, although leave may be granted in cases not specifically provided for under the law. But under the laws of the province there is an appeal from the final court of appeal of the province to His Majesty in his Privy Council; that we could not touch. Every litigant who goes to the Supreme Court makes his choice. He may go direct to his Majesty and not go to the Supreme Court at all or he may go to the Supreme Court, so it is not quite in our hands to determine whether there shall be, generally speaking, any appeal to His Majesty in his Privy Council. We have, so far as judgments of the Supreme Court are concerned, determined that there shall be no right of appeal and there is no right of appeal; but the Act saves any right which His Majesty may be pleased to exercise in virtue of his royal prerogative, so that there is an appeal only in so far as His Majesty, by royal prerogative, has a right to hear any appeal of any one of his subjects and an appeal only when he grants leave and chooses to exercise the right. It would involve a serious question whether we could legislate if we wanted to.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Could the Imperial parliament legislate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Imperial parliament legislate to take away the prerogative of His Majesty? I think that any prerogative of His Majesty may disappear by legislation, always provided that His Majesty is a party to that legislation; and, as an abstract question, I believe that this Parliament would have power to legislate and to do away with that right or with that prerogative of His Majesty, because His Majesty is part of this Parliament. No law affecting his prerogative would take effect any more than any other law without his assent. But I also think it is
Mr. DOHERTY.
very probable that if we did pass a law, and it was assented to by the Governor General as representing His Majesty, a serious question would arise as to whether His Majesty might not be advised by the United Kingdom Government to disallow that Act, as it would be within his power to do. If I am not mistaken, I believe that that very question arose, and was discussed, at the time of the enactment of the Supreme Court Act. However all this is something with which we cannot deal in this Bill.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: I think you will find that I am right if you consult persons interested in art. For that reason I was going .to make the suggestion that the composition of the board be such that men like Sir William Van Horne or the president of the Royal Academy, or the rector of Laval University, and other people whom I could name, might, in course of time, become members. Unless there are very good reasons for restricting the number to five. I would suggest that the question be left open.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: There must be some limit. It would be a very poor arrangement to have the number unlimited. I think we had better let it stand at five now, and we can change it next year if we think necessary.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: Would the minister accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that the gallery be open on Sunday? Since the suggestion was made, the press of the country has taken it up, and has viewed it very favourably. In fact, I have heard no dissenting voice I have read articles in Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa papers, all favouring the suggestion that this National Gallery should be open on Sundays, as all the great art collections in Europe are.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Personally I entirely
agree with the proposition made by my hon. friend from Simcoe. The matter has not yet been considered, but, so far as my recommendation would go, I would be glad to support it.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-objects and powers of board:

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: There was the question of real estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
I wish to propose an
amendment in the third line from the last, that after the word ' other ' we add the word 'similar.' The clause would then read in this way:
The custody and preservation of the works of art contributed by members of the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts to the National Gallery under the statute in that behalf; the acquiring by purchase, lease, devise or otherwise, of pictures, statuary, works of art, and other similar property.
And then leave out the balance of the clause.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
That will cover it.
Section, as amended, agreed .to.
On section 6-expenditure of moneys:

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
I suppose they would
come to Parliament each year and ask for the appropriation of a certain amount for the purposes of the board during that year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Yes, there will be an
amount in the estimates.
Section agreed, to.
On section 8-annual report:

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: Would such a monument as the one the contract for which was awarded to Mr. Allward, of Toronto, come under the direct jurisdiction of this board ? I think the hon. Minister of Public Works looked after the expenditure of that money in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
We continue to do sc,
but we ask the board to select.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Has the monument to the memory of King Edward been submitted to the present board ?
311*

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Yes, they made the
selection.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Some years ago we
gave a contract to Mr. Allward, who, I understand, is a very great sculptor, even a man of genius, for the monument to Baldwin and Lafontaine. Does the minister know what progress has been made with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: It has never been brought to my attention.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister inquire ?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
Yes. The preamble of
this Bill states that the National Gallery was established in the year 1880, and, as there is a difference of opinion as to whether it was established in 1880 or 1882. I move that the date be stricken out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext:
I trust the minister
will consider my suggestion before the third reading as to increasing the number of members on this hoard to seven instead of five.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: THE NATIONAL GALLERY.
speechtext: I do not object to that. I move that the Bill be amended by making the number seven.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported as amended; amendments concurred in, and Bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: PORT ARTHUR DRY-DOCK.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Robert Rogers, the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to ratify and confirm an agreement between the Western Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company, Limited, and His Majesty, dated the 9th day of November, 1910, respecting the construction of a dry-dock at the city of Port Arthur, in the province of Ontario, and to authorize the Governor in Council to pay an annual subsidy of three per cent per annum for twenty years upon the sum of $1,258,050, being the cost of the construction of the said dry-dock.

maintopic: PORT ARTHUR DRY-DOCK.
speechtext:
I understand that this
resolution is to confirm an agreement entered into in 1909 and is under the statute. I am content to have the resolution passed now, as the matter can be discussed on the second reading of the Bill.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. ROGERS thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 206, to authorize the payment of a subsidy to the Western Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company Limited.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. Wednesday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Wednesday, May 14, 1913.
